PGS000929 is the better endpoint match to the target trait dementia: it is explicitly “All-cause dementia (algorithmically-defined)” with trait_efo=dementia, aligning directly with generic dementia risk. PGS000945 is dementia specifically “in Alzheimer’s disease (time-to-event)” (trait_efo includes Alzheimer disease) and its phenotyping_reported is TTE dementia in AD, which is a narrower, conditional endpoint and less faithful to all-cause dementia. Although PGS000945 reports materially stronger PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.753, R2 0.065) than PGS000929 (0.627, 0.023) with similar basic covariates and similar training/validation context, the phenotype mismatch (AD-conditioned TTE vs all-cause dementia) is the primary differentiator here, so PGS000929 wins on endpoint fidelity.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Nat Genet study, same method (PRS-CS), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same phenotyping_reported (Dilated cardiomyopathy), same covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), and same validation sample size (n=347,585), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not ideal for PRS comparison). PGS004862 is better supported because it is the MTAG-enhanced version (trait_reported: "Dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG)") which domain guidance mildly prefers over the base endpoint when otherwise comparable, and it also shows slightly stronger reported signals in the selected record (AUROC 0.71 vs 0.70; R² 0.05 vs 0.048; OR 1.76 vs 1.56). The edge is modest because the metrics are full-model and differences are small, hence moderate confidence.

PGS001331 is the better-supported choice for generic Crohn’s disease risk: it has a cleaner endpoint match (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported are plain Crohn’s disease) whereas PGS001330 is explicitly time-to-event (“TTE crohn’s disease [regional enteritis]”), which is a mild endpoint mismatch for a generic disease target. On PRS-comparable metrics, PGS001331 is also slightly stronger (PGS-only AUROC 0.57919 vs 0.57593; PGS-only R² 0.00677 vs 0.00621; incremental AUROC 0.02705 vs 0.02413) with identical training cohort (UKB), training N, covariates, and validation N, so the small but consistent performance edge plus better endpoint fidelity favors PGS001331.

Both candidates are near-clones: same reported trait (Major Depressive Disorder, lifetime), same EFO mapping, same phenotyping_reported, same method (PRSice-2), same training cohort (UKB) and training N (67,164), same covariates (PCs 1-10), same validation size (42,250) and identical multi-ancestry evaluation distribution. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R²; the only visible metric is a generic R² that appears to be full-model, so it is weak for PRS comparison. With endpoints and design effectively identical, the only differentiator is the slightly higher reported R² for PGS003580 (0.0254) vs PGS003576 (0.0241), so PGS003580 edges out, but the evidence gap is minimal.

PGS004947 is better supported for dilated cardiomyopathy because it reports PRS-comparable performance directly (explicit univariate/PRS-only AUC=0.66 with CI and delta PRS/residual liability-scale R²=0.076), whereas PGS004861 only shows full-model AUROC=0.70 and R²=0.048 without any PRS-only metrics (so its AUC is not comparable as a standalone PRS signal). Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (both map to dilated cardiomyopathy EFO), and PGS004947’s phenotyping_reported as non-ischemic DCM remains a close clinical match; covariates are similarly basic in both. Although PGS004861 has larger EUR validation (n=347,585 vs n=96,016) and EUR-only evaluation, PGS004947’s clearer PRS-only evidence plus stronger per-SD OR (1.73 vs 1.56) and larger variant count (1,072,247 vs 713,932) outweigh that.

PGS004614 is the better-supported choice for generic diverticular disease because its endpoint is a direct disease diagnosis match (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Diverticular disease”) and it comes from a disease-focused diverticular-disease GWAS paper, with broad multi-ancestry evaluation listed (AFR/EUR/SAS). Although it only reports a full-model AUROC (0.76) and lacks PRS-only metrics, PGS000997’s key advantage is explicit PRS-only AUROC/R2 (0.591/0.0178), but it is a pan-trait UK Biobank “813 traits” sparse snpnet framework score with a time-to-event phenotype (“TTE diverticular disease of intestine”), which is a known weaker archetype for external generalization. Additionally, PGS004614’s reported covariates include family history (a comparability/leakage concern), but PGS000997’s framework origin and TTE packaging outweigh its cleaner covariate set given the target is generic diverticular disease.

Both candidates are essentially endpoint-identical for dupuytren contracture (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), come from the same UKB portability paper, have the same training size (n=391,124), covariates, ancestry distribution, and validation sample size (n=18,971), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so performance evidence is limited to very similar partial-r (0.0797 for PGS002092 vs 0.0783 for PGS001880). With endpoints and metrics near-tied, the structural signal breaks the tie: PGS002092 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (484,484 vs 2,443), which is generally favored for capturing polygenic signal when other evidence is indistinguishable. Confidence is moderate because the observed partial-r difference is tiny and both are from the same framework context.

PGS004947 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports an explicit univariate (PRS-only) AUC of 0.66 (with CI) and PRS delta R² metrics (e.g., liability-scale delta PRS/residual R²=0.076), whereas PGS004862 provides only full-model AUROC/R² (0.71/0.05) without any PRS-only metric, which the policy notes is not a valid substitute for PRS discrimination. Both use similar basic covariates (age, age^2, sex, PCs) with no obvious clinical leakage. Endpoint fidelity slightly favors PGS004862 (phenotyping_reported: dilated cardiomyopathy) over PGS004947 (non-ischemic DCM subtype), but the subtype mismatch is modest and outweighed by PGS004947’s cleaner PRS-isolated metrics and larger variant count (1,072,247 vs 709,534). Ancestry context is mixed (PGS004947 evaluated in MAE only vs PGS004862 in EUR), lowering confidence, but the presence of PRS-only metrics still makes PGS004947 the stronger-supported record overall.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target depressive disorder: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (lifetime MDD), same method (PRSice-2), same training cohort (UKB) and training N (67,164), same covariates (PCs 1-10), same ancestry distribution and validation sample size (42,250), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only a generic R² that appears to be full-model/non-PRS-comparable). With endpoint fidelity and study design indistinguishable, the only visible differentiators are small full-model R² (0.0257 for PGS003578 vs 0.0241 for PGS003576) and variant count (4,786,322 vs 5,776,312). Given domain guidance that small full-model R² differences are essentially noise when PRS-only metrics are absent, I give a slight edge to PGS003578 for the marginally higher reported R², but confidence is low because the evidence is effectively tied and the metric is not clearly PRS-only.

PGS004614 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (diverticular disease) because it is disease-focused with exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Diverticular disease”) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with very large variant coverage (1,082,282), plus multi-ancestry evaluation is indicated. Although its only reported AUROC (0.76) is a full-model metric and is likely inflated by explicit family-history covariate inclusion (so not PRS-comparable), the competing PGS000996 is a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse snpnet score (“across 813 traits”) with very weak PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.5519; PGS R2 0.00372) and a slightly broader/combined phenotype (“Diverticular disease/diverticulitis”), which is less endpoint-faithful to the specific target. Net: despite missing PRS-only metrics for PGS004614, the framework-penalty and weak PRS-only evidence for PGS000996 make PGS004614 the stronger candidate.

Both candidates align well to the target (same trait_efo: Dupuytren Contracture; phenotyping_reported is a direct Dupuytren/contracture diagnosis in both). PGS001254 has clearly reported PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.6646 and PGS-only R² 0.0247), whereas PGS002092 reports only partial correlation (partial-r 0.0797) and has no PGS-only AUC/R², making its predictive strength harder to judge. Although PGS002092 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with many variants and includes multi-ancestry evaluation, the absence of standard PRS-only discrimination metrics on the record leaves weaker direct evidence than PGS001254’s explicit PRS-only AUROC/R²; hence PGS001254 is better-supported on visible fields.

Both candidates are near-clones: same reported trait (MDD lifetime), same EFO mapping, same phenotyping_reported, same method (PRSice-2), identical variant count, identical training cohort (UKB) and training N, identical covariates (PCs 1-10), identical ancestry distribution and validation sample size. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R²; both only show a full-model R², which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric. With endpoint fidelity and study design indistinguishable, the only visible differentiator is the slightly higher reported R² in PGS003578 (0.0257 vs 0.0254 for PGS003580), so PGS003578 wins on marginally stronger performance evidence, though confidence is low because the difference is tiny and based on full-model R².

PGS000997 is better supported for the target trait (diverticular disease) because it has stronger PRS-comparable performance on the selected European validation record (PGS-only AUROC 0.591 and PGS-only R2 0.0178) than PGS000996 (PGS-only AUROC 0.552 and R2 0.0037), with both using similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs) and the same pan-trait UKB framework context. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both, but PGS000997 maps cleanly to diverticular disease of intestine (EFO diverticular disease), whereas PGS000996 mixes diverticular disease/diverticulitis (broader/combined EFO). The higher variant count in PGS000997 (5757 vs 368) is a supportive within-method structural advantage consistent with its better PRS-only metrics. Heritability sanity-check is also consistent: PGS000997’s PGS-only R2 (~0.018) aligns with the diverticular disease h2_liability (~0.017) ceiling more plausibly than PGS000996’s much smaller R2, reinforcing that PGS000997 captures more of the available genetic signal.

PGS005170 is better supported for the target trait (dementia) on endpoint fidelity and study archetype: it targets incident all-cause dementia (trait_efo=dementia) and comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort integrative PRS (24-component ensemble; 1.32M variants) with multi-ancestry evaluation reported. Although it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (only a full-model AUROC=0.761 plus HR=1.25) and includes APOE allele dosage as a covariate (which can dilute PRS-only interpretability), its phenotype is directly aligned to generic dementia risk. In contrast, PGS000945 is from a pan-trait UKB framework paper (“across 813 traits”) using a very sparse snpnet model (26 variants) and its endpoint is narrower/more conditional (“dementia in Alzheimer’s disease” time-to-event), which is a weaker match to general dementia; despite having explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.753; PGS R²=0.065), it carries the framework/sparse-model generalization penalty and the phenotype mismatch. Overall, the cleaner dementia endpoint and disease-focused integrative construction outweigh the metric-availability advantage of the UKB framework score.

Both candidates are well-aligned to the target (same trait_efo: Dupuytren Contracture; phenotyping_reported is a direct Dupuytren/palmar fascia contracture endpoint in both). The key differentiator is that PGS001254 reports clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6646 and PGS R2 (no covariates)=0.0247) in a European evaluation, whereas PGS001880 provides no PRS-only AUROC/R2 and only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0783), which is less directly comparable for PRS discrimination. Although PGS001880 has a larger variant set (2443 vs 11) and broader multi-ancestry evaluation, the absence of standard PRS-only AUC/R2 evidence makes it harder to judge and support over PGS001254’s explicit PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (trait_efo=follicular lymphoma; trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Nodular lymphoma”), from the same publication, with identical EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, identical training (n=3,696; MGI), identical covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and identical validation size (n=3,256). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use PRS-comparable discrimination; only full-model AUROC is shown and is not a clean PRS metric. Given this near-tie, PGS000644 has slightly better reported full-model AUROC (0.538 vs 0.532) and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.149 vs 1.133), plus a larger variant count (2,209,179 vs 1,048,780), so it edges PGS000643 on the limited visible evidence.

PGS002304 is the better-supported match for the target trait because its endpoint fidelity is exact across fields (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both “Follicular lymphoma”), whereas PGS000643 is labeled/phenotyped as “Nodular lymphoma” despite mapping to the same EFO, creating avoidable ambiguity for a follicular lymphoma target. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show full-model AUROC), so performance comparability is weak; the higher full-model AUROC in PGS002304 (0.61 vs 0.532) is only mildly supportive given unknown covariates, but it does not conflict with any disclosed heavy clinical packaging. PGS000643 has cleaner disclosed covariates (age/sex/PCs) and a genome-wide PRS-CS construction with many variants, but its phenotype label mismatch versus the target outweighs those structural advantages under the endpoint-fidelity-first policy.

Both candidates match the target well at the concept level (trait_reported and trait_efo are Primary open-angle/open-angle glaucoma). However, PGS001797 provides a PRS-comparable performance metric (PGS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.031479), which is interpretable and below the glaucoma heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0556), whereas PGS004944 reports no PRS-only AUC/R2 and only a full-model AUROC (0.748) that is not comparable as a standalone PRS metric. PGS004944 does have a strong per-SD OR (1.74) and broader multi-ancestry evaluation, but its endpoint is explicitly self-reported and its key performance evidence is full-model only; overall the cleaner PRS-specific metric support favors PGS001797.

Both candidates target the same endpoint clinically (phenotyping_reported and trait_reported are Primary open-angle glaucoma) and use the same method (PRS-CS-auto) with similar genome-wide variant counts, so performance evidence is the main differentiator. PGS001792 has slightly stronger PRS-comparable performance (pgs_only_r2 0.03209 vs 0.031479 for PGS001797) and a higher reported AUROC in the selected record (0.777 vs 0.749), while covariates are still basic in both (demographics + PCs; PGS001792 adds age^2 and interactions but no clear leakage). Although PGS001797 lists more development cohorts, its validation is much smaller (n=7,128 vs n=347,396), and given near-clone status the modest but consistent metric edge favors PGS001792.

Both candidates target primary open-angle glaucoma, but PGS001792 has cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports a covariates-regressed-out/PGS-only Nagelkerke R2 of 0.03209, which is interpretable as PRS signal and is below the glaucoma liability h2 ceiling (~0.0556). In contrast, PGS004944 provides no PGS-only AUC/R2 and only a full-model AUROC (0.748), which is not comparable as a standalone PRS metric even though it reports a strong OR (1.74). PGS001792 also has broader, explicitly multi-cohort development (BBJ, BioMe, TWB, UCLA) and a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) with higher variant count, while PGS004944’s evidence is more limited/less directly comparable due to reliance on full-model AUROC and self-reported phenotyping.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (trait_efo = Hashimoto's thyroiditis; phenotyping_reported/trait_reported = lymphocytic thyroiditis) with the same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry mix, same validation sample size (n=94,651), and unknown covariates; neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative. Given otherwise matched endpoint and study context, PGS005271 has consistently stronger visible performance signals than PGS005272: higher reported AUROC (0.6297 vs 0.6054) and stronger per-SD effect sizes (OR 1.55 vs 1.42; beta 0.438 vs 0.349). Variant counts are essentially identical and not decisive. Therefore PGS005271 is better-supported on the available fields.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment to gout (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and only basic covariates. However, PGS001789 provides an explicit PRS-comparable metric (Nagelkerke’s R2 with covariates regressed out / PGS-only R2 = 0.0312), which is interpretable and below the gout heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0525), whereas PGS004266 reports only full-model AUROC/pseudo-R2 (no PGS-only AUC/R2), making its performance evidence less comparable for PRS quality. Additionally, PGS001789 is developed across many biobanks with multi-ancestry GWAS input and multi-ancestry evaluation, supporting transportability, while PGS004266 is UKB EUR-only development/evaluation with a sparse 200-variant score. Overall, PGS001789 is better-supported on PRS-relevant metrics and external/ancestry breadth.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all = gout) and use only basic covariates. However, PGS001248 provides PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.669 and PGS-only R2=0.040), whereas PGS004266 reports only full-model AUROC/pseudo-R2 with no PGS-only AUC/R2, which the policy says should not be substituted as comparable PRS evidence. PGS001248 also shows broader evaluation ancestry (EUR plus AFR/EAS/SAS) versus PGS004266 EUR-only, supporting better transportability evidence. Despite PGS001248 coming from a pan-trait UKB framework paper (a negative signal), the lack of PRS-only metrics for PGS004266 leaves weaker direct support, so PGS001248 is better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates have clean endpoint fidelity for gout (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and use only basic demographic/PC-style covariates. However, PGS001248 comes from the explicit pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse snpnet framework (a known underperforming archetype for external generalization), whereas PGS001789 is from a global multi-biobank PRS development/benchmarking context with many contributing cohorts and a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS-auto) and much broader GWAS ancestry input. Although PGS001248 reports slightly higher PRS-comparable metrics in Europeans (PGS-only R2=0.040 vs 0.031 for PGS001789, and PGS-only AUROC=0.669 which PGS001789 lacks), that advantage is modest and the missing PGS-only AUROC for PGS001789 prevents over-weighting full-model AUROC. Given the strong framework penalty for the 813-traits sparse UKB score and the stronger multi-cohort, genome-wide construction of PGS001789, PGS001789 is better-supported overall.

Both candidates have identical endpoint alignment to the target (trait_efo Hashimoto's thyroiditis; phenotyping_reported lymphocytic thyroiditis), same publication family, same evaluation ancestry mix, and same validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). With comparable phenotype/transportability evidence, structural and PRS-signal evidence breaks the tie: PGS005271 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRSCS) with 1,085,156 variants and shows a much stronger per-SD effect size (OR≈1.55) than PGS005270 (P+T, 55 variants; OR≈1.04), suggesting materially stronger standalone PRS signal despite PGS005270’s slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.639 vs 0.630), a difference that is likely noise and not PRS-specific.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity for the target (trait_efo=Hashimoto's thyroiditis; trait_reported/phenotyping_reported=lymphocytic thyroiditis), same publication family, same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%) and same validation sample size (n=94,651), with covariates unknown in both—so phenotype/transportability do not differentiate. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC advantage of PGS005270 (0.639 vs 0.605) is discounted as non-comparable PRS evidence. Under the fallback when PRS-only metrics are absent, PGS005272 is better supported structurally and by PRS signal: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRSCS) with far more variants (1,085,142 vs 55) and shows a much stronger per-SD effect size (OR≈1.42 vs 1.04), indicating materially stronger discriminative power than the sparse P+T score PGS005270.

Both candidates align well to the target trait (trait_reported/trait_efo = heart failure). However, PGS001790 provides a clearly PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2 = 0.006981), which can be sanity-checked against the trait heritability ceiling and is more informative for PRS quality than full-model AUROC. In contrast, PGS005097 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.72) with no PGS-only AUC/R2, making its discrimination evidence largely non-comparable for PRS ranking. While PGS005097 has a more diverse evaluation ancestry and higher variant count, the lack of PRS-only performance metrics and its ‘prevalent heart failure’ endpoint do not outweigh PGS001790’s explicit PRS-only R2 evidence.

PGS005097 is the better-supported match to the target trait (heart failure) on endpoint fidelity and study archetype: it directly targets “Heart failure” with phenotyping_reported “Prevalent heart failure” and comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort heart-failure genetics paper with broad development cohorts (BBJ, BioMe, CKB, FinnGen, GBMI, HERMES, MVP, etc.) and a large validation (n=40,989). PGS005083 is a narrower phecode-defined subtype label (“Congestive heart failure (CHF), NOS (PheCode 428.1)”) from a methods/portability comparison paper and is trained only in MVP, which is weaker external-support context despite having an OR per SD (1.455) and a higher reported full-model C-index (0.754 vs 0.72). Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model metrics are not decisive; with similar basic covariates, the stronger endpoint alignment and multi-cohort disease-focused evidence favor PGS005097.

PGS000726 is the better-supported match to the target trait (cirrhosis of liver): its trait_efo is exactly "cirrhosis of liver" and phenotyping_reported is the generic diagnosis "Cirrhosis", whereas PGS000704 targets the narrower subtype "Alcoholic cirrhosis" (trait_efo "alcoholic liver cirrhosis"), which is a phenotype mismatch for a generic cirrhosis endpoint. Neither record reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS000704’s reported C-index=0.711 is a full-model metric and not comparable as PRS evidence; by contrast PGS000726 provides more directly PRS-informative effect-size evidence (OR per SD 1.32 and OR top20% vs bottom20% 2.26). Study/transportability context also favors PGS000726: it is developed across multiple cohorts/biobanks (ACG, ARIC, BBJ, BioVU, FinnGen, PHB, UKB) with multi-ancestry evaluation listed, while PGS000704 is UKB-only development with limited evaluation ancestry breadth. Confidence is moderate because both lack clean PRS-only discrimination metrics.

PGS002763 has better endpoint fidelity to the target trait: its phenotyping_reported is directly “Hip osteoarthritis,” matching trait_reported/trait_efo, whereas PGS002728 uses “Total hip replacement,” a treatment/proxy endpoint that can reflect access/surgical decision and disease severity rather than hip OA status. Neither record provides PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (PGS002728’s AUROC=0.66 is full-model and not a valid substitute for PGS-only), but PGS002763 at least reports a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.38, 95% CI 1.31–1.46) supporting PRS signal. Structurally, PGS002763 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.05M variants versus 44 GWAS-significant variants for PGS002728, which is generally favorable for a polygenic disease like hip OA. PGS002728’s multi-cohort development is supportive, but it does not outweigh the proxy endpoint and lack of PRS-only metrics.

PGS000967 has directly comparable PRS-only performance reported (PGS AUROC no covariates=0.5611; PGS R2 no covariates=0.00628), which is interpretable and sits below the hip OA heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0219), whereas PGS002728 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.66) with no PGS-only AUC/R2, so its discrimination cannot be attributed to the PRS. Endpoint fidelity is mixed for both: PGS000967 uses a time-to-event hip OA diagnosis (coxarthrosis), while PGS002728 uses total hip replacement (a proxy/treatment endpoint). Although PGS002728 is from a disease-focused OA risk paper, the lack of PRS-comparable metrics plus the THR proxy endpoint makes it less well-supported on the visible fields than PGS000967’s cleaner PRS-only metrics and broader multi-ancestry evaluation.

PGS001790 is the better-supported heart-failure PRS because it reports a PRS-comparable metric (Nagelkerke’s R2 with covariates regressed out / PGS-only R2 = 0.006981), which is directly usable for PRS ranking and is plausibly below the heart-failure heritability ceiling noted in the context. It also has clean endpoint alignment (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Heart failure”) and a very broad multi-cohort development context (many biobanks), albeit evaluated only in EUR. In contrast, PGS005083 targets a narrower phecode-defined CHF NOS endpoint (still related but less direct to generic ‘heart failure’) and provides no PRS-only AUC/R2; its only discrimination metric is a full-model C-index (~0.754), which is not comparable as a PRS metric, even though it does report a reasonably strong OR per SD (1.455) and has multi-ancestry evaluation. Given the lack of PRS-only performance for PGS005083, PGS001790 has the cleaner, more directly comparable evidence package.

PGS000644 is better supported as a standalone PRS for the target endpoint despite the slightly noisier label: its phenotyping_reported (“Nodular lymphoma”) maps to the same EFO concept (follicular lymphoma; ICD10 C82 includes “follicular [nodular]”), and it provides PRS-relevant effect-size evidence (OR per SD 1.149, with beta/SE) plus a clearly described basic covariate set (age, sex, batch, PCs), reducing comparability/leakage concerns. PGS002304 has exact trait/phenotype wording (“Follicular lymphoma”) and a higher reported AUROC (0.61 vs 0.538), but this AUROC is full-model (no PGS-only metrics) with covariates listed as “Unknown,” making the performance less interpretable; it is also an extremely sparse 6-variant GWS score with no effect sizes shown, offering weaker evidence of capturing polygenic signal. With both lacking PGS-only AUC/R2, the cleaner covariate disclosure and richer PRS signal reporting favor PGS000644.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Hodgkin’s disease/lymphoma), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sizes (n=736 train; n=775 eval), and similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use PRS-comparable metrics and must treat the reported AUROC/R2 as full-model. Within this otherwise matched sibling pair, PGS000639 shows consistently stronger empirical performance/effect evidence than PGS000637: higher AUROC (0.62 vs 0.574), higher pseudo-R² (0.0276 vs 0.013), higher OR per SD (1.476 vs 1.3) and higher top-1% OR (2.64 vs 1.67). Although PGS000637 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method with many variants, the observed validation metrics favor PGS000639 in this specific head-to-head.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported = Hodgkin’s disease / Hodgkins lymphoma), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training n=736, same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation size (n=775). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use PRS-comparable metrics and must treat the full-model AUROC as only weakly informative. Within this identical endpoint/covariate setting, PGS000639 shows consistently stronger performance/effect evidence than PGS000638: higher AUROC (0.62 vs 0.601), higher pseudo-R² (0.0276 vs 0.0193), higher OR per SD (1.476 vs 1.377), and higher top-1% OR (2.64 vs 1.62). It also has slightly more variants (20 vs 16). These aligned advantages make PGS000639 better supported overall.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = Hodgkin's disease; trait_efo = Hodgkins lymphoma), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), identical training cohort and size (MGI; n=736), identical covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and identical validation size (n=775). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use PRS-comparable metrics and must rely on the available full-model/effect-size evidence. PGS000638 shows consistently stronger reported performance than PGS000637 in the same evaluation setting: higher AUROC (0.601 vs 0.574) and higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0193 vs 0.013), with a slightly higher per-SD OR (1.377 vs 1.30). Given the near-clone design, these within-family metric differences favor PGS000638 despite PGS000637’s much larger variant count.

PGS001320 provides clean, PRS-comparable performance evidence (PGS-only AUROC=0.629 and PGS-only R²=0.06493 with explicit “no covariates” metrics), enabling a direct assessment of genetic signal and a heritability-ceiling sanity check. In contrast, PGS004234 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.763) with a heavier covariate set (including BMI, smoking, race/ethnic background, study site), and lacks any PGS-only AUROC/R² or effect sizes, so its discrimination is not comparable and may be largely covariate-driven. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (hypertension vs prevalent hypertension), but the decisive difference is that PGS001320 has standalone PRS metrics while PGS004234 does not.

Both candidates target Graves’ disease (a strong match to the broader hyperthyroidism target) with identical phenotyping_reported, EFO mapping, evaluation ancestry mix (MAE), and the same validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not PRS-comparable). Given this near-tie on endpoint and validation context, structural and effect-size evidence breaks the tie: PGS005266 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a much stronger per-SD effect (OR≈1.54, β≈0.434) than PGS005264’s very sparse P+T score (112 variants) with essentially null effect sizes (OR≈1.01, β≈0.008). The small full-model AUROC difference (0.664 vs 0.659) is minor and not decisive, but it is directionally consistent with PGS005266 being stronger.

Both candidates target the same trait (hypertension; EFO hypertension) with identical phenotyping_reported (“Prevelant hypertension”), identical covariates (age/sex/PCs plus smoking and BMI), and the same training N and validation N, so endpoint fidelity and covariate leakage risk do not differentiate them. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, and the full-model AUROC values are essentially identical (0.764 for PGS004236 vs 0.763 for PGS004234), so performance metrics are not a meaningful separator. PGS004236 is better supported because it provides a strong PRS-relevant effect size (OR 2.1 per SD, 95% CI 1.99–2.21), while PGS004234 reports no effect sizes; additionally, PGS004236 has broader development cohort support (BioMe, MVP, UKB vs BioMe, UKB) and a higher variant count (398,805 vs 234,228), which is a modest positive structural signal when other fields are near-tied.

Both candidates are near-clones: same target trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), same method (PRS-CS), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), same development cohorts, and same validation sample size (n=343,182). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC/R² are not ideal for PRS comparability, but within this matched setting PGS004911 shows consistently stronger reported performance/effect evidence than PGS004910 (AUROC 0.80 vs 0.73; R² 0.048 vs 0.031; HR 2.34 vs 1.97; OR per SD 1.33 vs 1.26; high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9 vs 5.5). Additionally, PGS004911 is the MTAG-enhanced version, which domain guidance mildly prefers over the base model when endpoint remains the same.

PGS002763 is the better-supported choice for the target trait hip osteoarthritis because its endpoint is a direct hip osteoarthritis diagnosis (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Hip osteoarthritis”) and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (1,052,273), plus a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.38, 95% CI 1.31–1.46) under basic covariates. In contrast, PGS000967 comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse framework (“across 813 traits”, snpnet) with a time-to-event phenotype (“TTE coxarthrosis”), which is a mild endpoint mismatch/packaging signal for a generic disease target, and its PRS-only metrics are weak (PGS-only AUROC=0.561, PGS R2=0.00628). Although PGS000967 reports explicit PRS-only AUC/R2 and has larger training/validation and multi-ancestry evaluation records, those advantages don’t outweigh the framework+sparse-method penalty and the weaker PRS-only signal versus the more disease-aligned, genome-wide score in PGS002763.

Both candidates have good endpoint fidelity (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), but PGS004911 is better-supported as a standalone PRS: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with 374,114 variants and reports PRS-linked effect sizes (HR=2.34, OR per SD=1.33; plus high-vs-median-tertile OR=5.9), with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), reducing covariate-driven inflation concerns. PGS000739 is a very sparse 27-variant GWS score and its reported AUROC=0.821 is from a model adjusted for multiple clinical risk factors plus rare-variant carrier status, making the full-model AUROC less comparable to PRS performance and more susceptible to clinical packaging/leakage. Neither provides PGS-only AUC/R2, so structural PRS quality and covariate cleanliness favor PGS004911 despite similar full-model AUROCs.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match disorders of iron metabolism), identical training cohort and size (UKB; n=391,124), identical covariates (sex, age, birth date, deprivation index, 16 PCs), and identical ancestry evaluation mix and validation N (n=19,883), so the decision rests on PRS-comparable performance and structural signals. PGS002031 shows slightly higher PRS-comparable partial correlation (partial-r 0.1355 vs 0.1307 for PGS001823) with overlapping but marginally better CI, and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with far more variants (6713 vs 654), which is a supportive tie-break when metrics are otherwise sparse. With no PGS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, these small but consistent advantages favor PGS002031.

PGS000965 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.689) and PGS-only R² (0.0727) plus incremental AUROC, whereas PGS004935 provides only a full-model AUROC (0.70) with no PGS-only AUC/R², which is not comparable for judging standalone PRS quality. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (hypothyroidism vs hypothyroidism/myxoedema), and both are UKB-trained with similar training N, but PGS000965 also shows broader evaluation ancestry coverage (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS) while PGS004935 is EUR-only. Despite the framework-paper penalty for PGS000965, the absence of PRS-only metrics in PGS004935 makes its support weaker overall.

PGS001320 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.629 and PGS-only R²=0.06493 (no covariates), enabling a clean PRS assessment and a heritability-ceiling sanity check. In contrast, PGS004236 reports only a full-model AUROC=0.764 (no PGS-only AUC/R²), so its discrimination is not comparable as a standalone PRS—especially given the heavier covariate set including BMI and smoking. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (hypertension), but PGS004236’s phenotyping is explicitly ‘Prevelant hypertension’ (packaged prevalence framing) while PGS001320 is a generic hypertension endpoint. Although PGS004236 is from a disease-focused multi-ethnic study and reports a strong OR=2.1, the lack of PRS-only metrics and covariate-heavy evaluation make its PRS strength less directly evidenced than PGS001320’s clean PGS-only metrics.

PGS000965 is better-supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.689) and PGS-only R² (0.0727), whereas PGS005218 provides no PGS-only AUC/R² and only a full-model AUROC (0.859) that is not comparable as a standalone PRS metric. Moreover, PGS005218’s covariates include near-outcome thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO), strongly suggesting the high AUROC is largely covariate-driven and thus weak evidence about PRS quality. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (hypothyroidism; PGS005218 is incident-only, PGS000965 is hypothyroidism/myxoedema), but the cleaner, directly interpretable PRS-only metrics in PGS000965 outweigh PGS005218’s larger multi-cohort training/validation and genome-wide variant count given the biomarker-heavy model packaging.

PGS000114 is the better match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis): its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to overall JIA, whereas PGS000325 is explicitly for the oligoarticular JIA subtype (endpoint mismatch for a broad JIA target). Both candidates come from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have similar basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and are EUR-only in development/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC), so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS000325 (0.80 vs 0.738) is discounted and not decisive. Given comparable study context and metrics, endpoint fidelity favors PGS000114.

Both candidates target Graves’ disease (a strong match to the hyperthyroidism umbrella) with identical phenotyping_reported, ancestry distribution, training cohort list, validation ancestry, and validation sample size, and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC is shown, so it’s weakly comparable). Given that, structural and effect-size evidence dominate: PGS005265 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRSCS) with ~1,085,173 variants and shows much stronger per-SD effect sizes (OR≈1.63, β≈0.49) than PGS005264’s sparse P+T score with 112 variants and near-null effect sizes (OR≈1.01, β≈0.008). The small full-model AUROC difference (0.665 vs 0.659) is minor, but it is directionally consistent with PGS005265 being stronger.

PGS000114 is the better match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are all the umbrella JIA endpoint, whereas PGS000326 is explicitly a subtype score (RF-negative polyarticular JIA) with a different trait_efo and phenotyping_reported. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show full-model AUROC), so performance is hard to compare cleanly; in that setting endpoint fidelity and effect-size support matter more. PGS000114 also shows a stronger per-SD OR (2.085 vs 1.51) and uses the same basic covariates and ancestry context as PGS000326, making the broader, target-aligned endpoint the deciding advantage.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target hyperthyroidism via the clinically dominant subtype Graves’ disease: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%), same validation sample size (n=94,651), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not PRS-comparable). With endpoint fidelity and evidence packaging essentially tied, PGS005265 has slightly stronger visible performance/effect-size signals than PGS005266 (full-model AUROC 0.6652 vs 0.6637; OR per SD 1.625 vs 1.543; β 0.486 vs 0.434) and a trivially higher variant count (1,085,173 vs 1,085,170), so it is marginally better-supported on the available fields.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/trait_efo are hypothyroidism). However, PGS005218’s only reported discrimination is a full-model AUROC=0.859 while explicitly adjusting for strong near-outcome thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO), making that AUROC largely non-comparable and potentially covariate-driven rather than PRS-driven. PGS004935, despite being a portability-style UKB-only score with smaller training/validation and unknown covariates, provides at least some PRS-specific evidence via an effect size (OR per SD=1.5, 95% CI 1.41–1.6), which is a meaningful indicator of PRS discriminative power when PGS-only AUC/R2 are absent. With no PGS-only AUC/R2 available for either, the biomarker-heavy covariate leakage in PGS005218 outweighs its higher full-model AUROC, so PGS004935 is better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates are from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have similar basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and are EUR-only in development/evaluation, so transportability and design are essentially tied. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC is shown, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric), so we lean on endpoint fidelity plus the available effect-size/discrimination evidence. PGS000325 targets an oligoarticular JIA subtype and shows stronger reported discrimination/effect size (AUROC 0.80 [0.77–0.84], OR 1.93 [1.75–2.13]) than PGS000326’s RF-negative polyarticular subtype (AUROC 0.76 [0.72–0.80], OR 1.51 [1.35–1.68]). With similar validation sizes, the materially stronger OR and AUROC support PGS000325 as the better-supported model for juvenile idiopathic arthritis risk in this head-to-head.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target trait (kidney cancer) because its endpoint is a direct match (phenotyping_reported: “Kidney cancer”; trait_efo: renal carcinoma) and it comes from a kidney-cancer–focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis, with a much stronger PRS effect size signal (OR 1.5 per SD, 95% CI 1.43–1.58) and a substantially larger variant set (107 vs 19). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC is shown), so the small AUROC difference (0.74 vs 0.722) is not a clean PRS comparator; in that setting, the stronger per-SD effect size and richer disease-focused evidence package favor PGS004908 over PGS000076, which is from a cross-cancer evaluation with an incident-only endpoint and a weaker HR (1.16).

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same trait_reported/phenotyping_reported (N18 chronic renal failure), same trait_efo (kidney failure), same publication, same training cohort (UKB), same training N and validation N, same EUR-only DEV/EVAL, and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only OR reported; covariates unknown for both). With metrics otherwise missing, the main differentiator is the reported per-SD effect size: PGS004562 shows a materially stronger OR (1.39548; moderate) than PGS004492 (1.1708; weak), and its method (RFDiseasemetaPRS) is consistent with multi-score aggregation, which is structurally favored over a single-score LDpred2 when endpoints are identical. Therefore PGS004562 is better supported on the visible evidence.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target “kidney cancer” because it is a disease-focused kidney cancer GWAS meta-analysis score (Nat Genet) with a much stronger PRS effect size signal (OR=1.5 per SD, 95% CI 1.43–1.58) and a substantially richer variant set (107 genome-wide significant SNPs) than PGS000787 (19 variants; HR=1.15 per SD, 1.07–1.24), which suggests weaker standalone PRS discrimination. Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC is shown), so the small full-model AUROC difference (0.74 vs 0.722) is not a reliable differentiator; thus effect size + disease-focused development context favors PGS004908. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (PGS000787 is renal cell carcinoma/incident kidney cancer—dominant subtype—while PGS004908 is kidney cancer/renal carcinoma), so the stronger genetic signal and more comprehensive GWAS-hits construction in PGS004908 breaks the tie.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer; EUR GWAS/EVAL). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as a PRS metric. Given that limitation, PGS004860 has stronger structural support for capturing polygenic signal (LDpred2 with 1,143,554 variants vs genome-wide significant hits with 109 variants in PGS000078) and a stronger per-SD effect size signal (OR=1.33 vs HR=1.16, indicating more discriminative PRS contribution). PGS000078 also has heavier covariate packaging (family history, PM2.5, detailed smoking interactions), making its full-model AUROC less informative about the PRS itself than PGS004860’s simpler covariate set.

Both candidates have identical endpoint alignment (trait_reported kidney cancer; trait_efo renal cell carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident kidney cancer), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/EVAL), identical covariates, identical variant count (19), and essentially identical full-model discrimination/effect size (AUROC 0.722; C-index ~0.723–0.724; HR per SD ~1.15–1.16). The key differentiator is that PGS000787 is explicitly derived from PGS000076 but with 'inverse variant weights', which is a red-flag packaging/implementation change with no shown PRS-only performance benefit (no PGS-only AUC/R2 for either). PGS000076 is the original genome-wide significant-variant score from the cross-cancer evaluation, making it the better-supported and less idiosyncratically modified record on the visible fields.

PGS001192 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence for knee osteoarthritis: it reports explicit PGS-only metrics (PGS AUROC(no covariates)=0.5566; PGS R2=0.0068), enabling a clean PRS assessment and a heritability-ceiling sanity check (R2 well below h2_obs≈0.0219). In contrast, PGS002729 provides only a full-model AUROC=0.66 with covariates (age/sex/BMI) and no PGS-only AUC/R2, so its apparent performance is not comparable as a standalone PRS signal. Endpoint mapping is acceptable for both (trait_efo osteoarthritis, knee), but PGS001192’s time-to-event phenotyping is a mild mismatch versus PGS002729’s generic clinical OA; this is outweighed by PGS001192’s clearer PRS-only performance reporting and stronger genome-wide model specification (4525 variants vs 24 GWAS hits).

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). Neither reports PRS-only AUROC/R², so the full-model AUROC values are not directly comparable as PRS metrics. However, PGS000739’s reported AUROC=0.821 is paired with heavy clinical covariates (multiple clinical risk factors plus rare-variant carrier status), making its discrimination likely covariate-driven and less informative for standalone PRS quality. In contrast, PGS004910 uses only basic demographic/PC covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10) and provides PRS effect-size evidence (OR per SD 1.26; HR 1.97; OR high vs median tertile 5.5) alongside a large EUR validation (n=343,182). Structurally, PGS004910 is a genome-wide shrinkage score (PRS-CS; 374,190 variants) versus a 27-variant GWAS-hits score for PGS000739, which is generally less able to capture polygenic signal for complex disease. Overall, PGS004910 is better-supported on cleaner evaluation design and stronger PRS-specific structural/effect-size evidence, while PGS000739’s apparent AUROC advantage is confounded by covariate packaging.

PGS002237 is better supported for the kidney-failure spectrum because it has clearer, richer validation evidence and broader transportability: it reports an AUROC (0.78, though it appears to be full-model rather than PGS-only) plus a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.47, CI 1.32–1.65) and is evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/AMR/ASN/EUR/MAE) with multiple performance records. In contrast, PGS004492 maps to kidney failure via ICD N18 chronic renal failure (reasonable alignment) and uses a strong genome-wide method (LDpred2) with many variants, but it provides only a modest OR (~1.17) and no AUC/R2/PGS-only metrics at all, with EUR-only evaluation and unknown covariates, leaving substantially weaker visible performance support.

PGS004562 is the better match to the target trait kidney failure on endpoint fidelity: its trait_efo is explicitly "kidney failure" and the reported/phenotyped endpoint is ICD code N18 chronic renal failure, which is closer to kidney failure than PGS002237’s "chronic kidney disease (stage 3 or greater)" with phenotyping based on eGFR<45 (CKD stage 3b+), a related but not equivalent endpoint. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS002237’s reported AUROC=0.78 is a full-model metric with extensive clinical/treatment covariates (hypertension, diabetes, BMI, NSAID and ACEi/ARB use, etc.), making it less comparable as PRS evidence; PGS004562 at least avoids explicit covariate-heavy packaging (covariates unknown) and provides a moderate OR (1.40). PGS002237 has stronger breadth signals (multi-ancestry evaluation, slightly higher OR 1.47), but given the target is kidney failure and the performance evidence is not PRS-clean, the closer endpoint alignment of PGS004562 narrowly wins.

Both candidates align to the target trait (systemic lupus erythematosus) at trait_reported/trait_efo, but PGS000196’s phenotyping_reported is narrower and potentially context-conditioned ("diagnosis in patient with arthritis"), whereas PGS000754 uses a straightforward SLE phenotype. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not PRS-comparable), so the higher full-model AUROC for PGS000196 (0.79 vs 0.65) is not a reliable differentiator. With metrics essentially non-comparable, structural signals dominate: PGS000754 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (lassosum) with far broader variant coverage (293,684 vs 55), which is generally better-supported for complex polygenic disease risk than a very sparse P+T score. PGS000754 also has much larger validation (n=7,733 vs n=245), which modestly increases trust once phenotype alignment is acceptable.

Both candidates map cleanly to systemic lupus erythematosus (trait_reported/trait_efo match), but PGS000754 has better endpoint fidelity for the generic target (“Systemic lupus erythematosus” phenotyping) whereas PGS000328 is restricted to early-onset SLE (onset before age 20), a narrower subtype for a generic “lupus erythematosus” target. Neither record reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.83 for PGS000328 vs 0.65 for PGS000754) are not PRS-comparable and shouldn’t drive selection. With metrics largely non-comparable, structural/transport signals favor PGS000754: a genome-wide lassosum score with far more variants (293,684 vs 57) and broader evaluation ancestry mix (includes EUR plus Asian groups) versus PGS000328’s EUR-only evaluation. Covariates are unknown for both, so no differentiator there.

Both candidates map cleanly to systemic lupus erythematosus (same trait_reported/trait_efo) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not PRS-comparable), so performance evidence is weakly differentiating. PGS000328 has a slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.83 vs 0.79) and larger validation n (1,001 vs 245), but its phenotyping_reported is restricted to early-onset SLE (onset before age 20), which is a narrower endpoint than the target ‘lupus erythematosus’. PGS000196 uses a more general clinical diagnosis context (‘SLE diagnosis in patient with arthritis’) and also shows some non-EUR evaluation (EUR+MAE), offering slightly broader transportability evidence. Given the target is generic lupus erythematosus and endpoint fidelity is the top criterion, PGS000196 is marginally better aligned despite the smaller validation and slightly lower full-model AUROC.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo is late-onset Alzheimer’s disease; phenotyping_reported is late-onset AD), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS000053 is better supported because it provides a PRS-relevant effect size (OR=1.29 per SD, 95% CI 1.21–1.37) with clean/basic covariates (age, sex) and is developed/validated across many AD-focused cohorts with EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry alignment. PGS000334’s only quantitative metric is an R²=0.191 reported under other_metrics with unknown covariates; given the trait heritability ceiling provided (h2_obs≈0.0084; h2_liability≈0.0269), this high R² is difficult to interpret and likely non-comparable (potentially full-model or otherwise inflated), so it is weaker evidence than the explicit OR in PGS000053.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and design: same trait_reported/trait_efo (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease), same phenotyping_reported (familial LOAD), same method (genome-wide significant variants) with the same variant count (21), same covariates (age, sex), and same multi-cohort development list from the same publication. Neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so performance must lean on the available effect size: PGS000054 shows a materially stronger per-score association (OR 1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93) than PGS000053 (OR 1.29, 1.21–1.37). Although PGS000053 has EUR evaluation (more aligned with the provided EUR heritability context) and a slightly larger validation n (4,792 vs 3,324), those are weak tie-breakers here versus the much stronger OR signal in PGS000054.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_efo is late-onset Alzheimer’s disease; phenotyping_reported is late-onset AD for PGS000334 and familial late-onset LOAD for PGS000054, which is still aligned). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so we rely on comparable evidence: PGS000054 provides a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93) with basic covariates (age, sex), which is informative for PRS discrimination. PGS000334 reports an R²=0.191 but it appears under other_metrics with full_model_r2 present and covariates listed as unknown, making the metric’s PRS-only comparability unclear and the magnitude suspiciously high relative to the provided heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0084; h2_liability≈0.0269), suggesting possible scale/covariate inflation. Given cleaner interpretability and stronger, clearly PRS-linked effect-size evidence, PGS000054 is better supported than PGS000334.

PGS004860 has better endpoint fidelity to the generic target trait (phenotyping_reported: incident lung cancer) and a cleaner, more standard lung-cancer covariate set (age/sex/BMI/smoking status + PCs) without explicit family-history/clinical-predictor packaging. PGS000740 is explicitly restricted to early-onset lung cancer (<50 years), which is a meaningful mismatch for general lung cancer risk, and it uses heavier clinical covariates (including family history of lung cancer and lung function), making its full-model AUROC (0.811) less informative for PRS quality. Neither record reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC for PGS004860 (0.893) cannot be treated as a PRS-comparable advantage, but combined with its genome-wide LDpred2 construction (1.14M variants vs 128) and cleaner endpoint/covariates, PGS004860 is better-supported overall.

PGS000078 is the better-supported choice for the generic target trait “lung cancer” because its endpoint is an unrestricted incident lung cancer phenotype (phenotyping_reported: “Incident lung cancer”), whereas PGS000740 is explicitly restricted to “Early onset lung cancer (< 50 years),” which is a meaningful endpoint mismatch for a general lung cancer target. Neither record reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (both have only full-model AUROC), so the higher full-model AUROC for PGS000078 (0.846 vs 0.811) is only weakly informative; however, PGS000078 at least provides an HR per SD (1.16) as PRS-relevant evidence, while PGS000740 provides no effect size. Both use covariates that include family history (and PGS000078 also includes extensive smoking/environment terms), making full-model AUROC less comparable, but the stronger phenotype alignment and presence of PRS effect-size evidence favor PGS000078 despite PGS000740’s somewhat broader evaluation ancestry.

Both candidates match the target conceptually (trait_reported and trait_efo are knee osteoarthritis), but PGS002767 has better PRS-structure evidence and cleaner covariate framing: it is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with ~1,052,275 variants and reports a standalone PRS effect size (OR 1.35, 95% CI 1.30–1.40) with only basic demographic/PC/technical covariates. In contrast, PGS002729 is a 24-variant genome-wide-significant score and the only discrimination metric shown is a full-model AUROC=0.66 with covariates including BMI (no PGS-only AUROC/R2), making the metric less PRS-comparable; it also has a less specific phenotyping label (“Clinical osteoarthritis”) versus knee-specific. Given no PGS-only AUC/R2 for either, the stronger genome-wide method/variant coverage plus knee-specific phenotype support PGS002767 over the sparse, covariate-influenced AUROC evidence in PGS002729.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo=lymphoid leukemia; phenotyping_reported=Incident Lymphocytic Leukemia) and use similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs) with identical EUR-only evaluation and the same validation sample size (n=391,338). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative; still, PGS000788 shows consistently stronger available signals than PGS000077 (higher full-model AUROC 0.738 vs 0.719; higher C-index 0.756 vs 0.735; stronger HR per SD 1.70 vs 1.45). The main drawback is that PGS000788 is a reweighted derivative of PGS000077 (“inverse variant weights”), making this close; but given the stronger effect size/discrimination with comparable endpoint/covariates, PGS000788 edges out.

PGS002767 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (knee osteoarthritis) because its endpoint fidelity is direct and generic (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Knee osteoarthritis”), whereas PGS001192 is explicitly a time-to-event (TTE) gonarthrosis endpoint, which is a weaker match for a generic disease-risk target. Although PGS001192 reports PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.5566; PGS R2 0.0068, plausibly below the h2_obs ceiling ~0.022) and has broader evaluation ancestries, it comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”, snpnet, 4,525 variants), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable externally than disease-focused/direct-endpoint scores. PGS002767 also provides a moderate per-SD effect size (OR 1.35, 95% CI 1.3–1.4) with clean basic covariates and a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS, ~1.05M variants), but lacks AUC/R2, lowering certainty—hence Moderate confidence.

PGS000788 is the better match to the target trait (lymphoid leukemia): its trait_efo is exactly “lymphoid leukemia” and phenotyping_reported is “Incident Lymphocytic Leukemia,” aligning to the broader lymphoid leukemia concept, whereas PGS000648 is explicitly for the subtype “chronic lymphocytic leukemia” (trait_efo chronic lymphocytic leukemia). Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC/R² are not comparable PRS metrics; however, PGS000788 at least reports a strong per-SD effect size (HR=1.7) with only basic covariates, while PGS000648’s evidence is tied to a smaller, single-cohort development context (MGI; samples_training n=730) and a narrower endpoint. Overall, endpoint fidelity to the requested umbrella trait favors PGS000788 despite both lacking clean PRS-only discrimination metrics.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo (melanoma), identical endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported: incident invasive melanoma), same covariates (age, sex), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same validation sample size (n=4,765), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC/R², which is not a clean PRS-comparable differentiator). Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/trait_efo = melanoma) and are EUR-only GWAS/EVAL with the same method family (genome-wide significant variants) and no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported, so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS-comparable differentiator. Endpoint fidelity slightly favors PGS002246 because it specifies the clinically tighter phenotype "incident invasive melanoma" versus PGS000079's broader "incident melanoma". With similar (basic) covariate burden overall (PGS002246: age, sex; PGS000079: age/sex/PCs/array plus UV-behavior/tanning covariates), PGS002246 also has a larger variant set (50 vs 24), a meaningful within-method structural advantage. PGS000079’s very large validation N and reported HR=1.43 are supportive, but the heavier non-genetic covariates and cross-cancer evaluation framing make its full-model AUROC less directly informative for PRS quality than the more melanoma-focused evaluation record in PGS002246.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/trait_efo = melanoma) and are EUR-only GWAS/EVAL with the same method family (genome-wide significant variants), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS-comparable differentiator). PGS004607 is a disease-focused, endpoint-faithful score for age-related macular degeneration (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align tightly to AMD) and reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.48, near the ≥1.5 “strong” guideline) with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs). Although it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (only a full-model AUROC=0.65, which is not PRS-comparable), its study context (Nat Genet AMD across ancestries; genome-wide PRS-CS with 1,067,520 variants) provides stronger structural and disease-specific support than PGS001013. PGS001013 comes from a pan-trait UKB sparse framework (“813 traits” snpnet) with very low variant count (53) and modest PRS-only performance (PGS AUROC 0.553; PGS R² 0.006), suggesting weak standalone PRS signal despite having explicit PRS-only metrics. Overall, the combination of tighter AMD endpoint fidelity and stronger disease-focused evidence favors PGS004607.

Both candidates target the exact same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all age-related macular degeneration) and use similarly clean covariates (age, sex, PCs 1–10) with the same EUR evaluation sample size (n=163,011), so endpoint fidelity and covariate leakage do not differentiate them. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC is only weakly informative; still, PGS004606 shows higher AUROC (0.71 vs 0.65) and a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.76 [1.73–1.78] vs 1.48 [1.34–1.63]), which is a more PRS-relevant signal. Additionally, PGS004606 is trained on EUR GWAS (IAMDGC) matching the EUR evaluation ancestry, whereas PGS004607 is trained on AFR GWAS (MVP) but evaluated in EUR, a transportability mismatch that plausibly contributes to its weaker effect size/performance. Overall, PGS004606 is better supported on the visible discrimination evidence and ancestry compatibility.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Multiple myeloma”, trait_efo plasma cell myeloma) and both are EUR-only with basic covariates (no obvious clinical leakage). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative; still, PGS002281 shows materially stronger validation discrimination (AUROC 0.644, OR highest vs lowest quintile 3.18) than PGS000653 (AUROC 0.577, top 1% OR 2.2 with wide CI crossing 1). Variant counts are similar (23 vs 22). PGS000653 has clearer training cohort metadata (UKB; n=3,377), but that is a weak differentiator versus the stronger observed performance signals for PGS002281.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment to multiple sclerosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and both are UKB-based framework-style scores with only basic demographic/PC covariates (no obvious clinical leakage). The key differentiator is comparable PRS performance evidence: PGS001270 reports explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6586; PGS R2 no covariates=0.0290), which are interpretable and sit plausibly below the provided liability-scale heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.117). In contrast, PGS002038 provides no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 at all (only partial correlation 0.0396), making its predictive support less directly comparable/usable despite higher variant count and larger training N. Therefore PGS001270 is better-supported on the visible record fields.

PGS001270 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (multiple sclerosis) because it matches the generic disease endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: “Multiple sclerosis”) whereas PGS001271 is explicitly a time-to-event formulation (“Multiple sclerosis (time-to-event)”, phenotyping_reported: “TTE multiple sclerosis”), which is a mild endpoint-fidelity penalty for a generic disease-risk target. Both candidates come from the same pan-trait UKB framework paper, use the same method (snpnet), identical covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), identical training size/cohort (UKB; n=269,704), and identical evaluation setup/size (n=67,425; same ancestry distribution), so performance metrics are the main differentiator: PGS001270 has higher PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.6586 vs 0.6469; PGS-only R² 0.0290 vs 0.0256) and slightly higher incremental AUROC (0.0836 vs 0.0715). Both R² values are below the provided heritability ceiling, so no metric-sanity issues; overall PGS001270 has cleaner endpoint alignment and stronger PRS-only performance.

Both candidates are near-clones: same myocardial infarction PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same method (ldpred), same variant count (1,286,612), same cohorts (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distribution, and same validation sample size (n=30,379). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model C-index is only weakly informative. Given otherwise identical support, PGS005039 has slightly stronger reported discrimination/effect evidence (full-model C-index 0.7848 vs 0.7834; OR per SD 1.578 vs 1.541), so it edges PGS005035, but the difference is small so confidence is low.

PGS001271 has cleaner, directly PRS-comparable performance reported for multiple sclerosis: it provides PGS-only AUROC=0.64688 and PGS-only R²=0.02562 (both explicitly no-covariates), enabling an interpretable comparison and a heritability-ceiling sanity check (well below h2_liability≈0.117). PGS002038 is endpoint-aligned but lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² entirely and reports only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0396), which is less directly comparable as a PRS discrimination metric. While PGS002038 has a stronger structural setup (LDpred2 with ~129k variants vs a very sparse 36-variant snpnet score) and similar basic covariates, the absence of standard PRS-only metrics makes its support weaker on the visible fields, so PGS001271 is better-supported overall.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (multiple myeloma / plasma cell myeloma), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (UKB) and training N=3,377, same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs1-4), and same validation N=2,738. Both candidates are near-clones: same myocardial infarction PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported match), same method (ldpred), same variant count (1,286,612), same cohorts (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distribution and validation sample size (n=30,379), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). Both candidates are near-clones: same MI PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same method (ldpred), same variant count (1,286,612), same cohorts (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distribution, and same validation sample size (n=30,379).
