Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (ICD10 J33 nasal polyp; EFO Nasal Cavity Polyp), same publication, same EUR-only training/validation context (UKB; n=174,489 train, n=56,192 eval), same variant count, and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only OR reported; covariates unknown). With metrics otherwise missing/indistinguishable, the tie-break is the available effect size: PGS004535 reports a stronger per-SD OR (1.60, in the ‘strong’ range) than PGS004465 (OR 1.35, moderate), providing better direct evidence of PRS discrimination despite PGS004465’s method label (LDpred2) being structurally appealing.

PGS004606 is a disease-focused age-related macular degeneration score with tight endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all AMD) and strong PRS signal via effect size (OR per SD 1.76, a strong discriminator), developed in an AMD consortium context (IAMDGC) with basic covariates only (age/sex/PCs). Although it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 and only reports a full-model AUROC=0.71 (not directly comparable), the available evidence is coherent and disease-specific. In contrast, PGS001013 comes from a pan-trait UKB framework (“across 813 traits”), uses a very sparse 53-variant snpnet model, and while it reports PRS-comparable metrics, they are weak (PGS-only AUROC 0.553; PGS R2 0.006), suggesting limited standalone PRS value despite a similar full-model AUROC driven largely by covariates. Overall, the stronger endpoint fidelity and effect-size evidence plus disease-focused study archetype favor PGS004606 over the weak PRS-only performance and framework-origin limitations of PGS001013.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo identical; phenotyping_reported identical albeit misspelled), use the same method (PRSCS), have the same evaluation ancestry mix and the same validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). With endpoint and design essentially tied, the differentiators are small but consistently favor PGS005262: it shows slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.5933 vs 0.5876) and stronger effect sizes (OR per SD 1.408 vs 1.362; beta 0.342 vs 0.309), plus a trivially higher variant count (1,085,173 vs 1,085,170) and a slightly broader listed training cohort set. Given the lack of PRS-only metrics, confidence is moderate rather than high.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate multiple myeloma / plasma cell myeloma) and both lack PRS-only AUROC/R², so full-model AUROC is only weakly comparable. However, PGS002281 comes from a disease-focused multiple-myeloma PRS paper and shows stronger reported discrimination in its selected European validation (full-model AUROC 0.644; OR highest vs lowest quintile 3.18) with only basic covariates (age/sex/region). PGS000654 is from a broader cancer PRS repository framework and has weaker reported performance (full-model AUROC 0.576; top 1% OR 2.2 with wide CI crossing 1) despite similarly basic covariates. With endpoints and ancestry essentially tied, the stronger effect-size and AUROC evidence favors PGS002281.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo match; phenotyping_reported identical aside from spelling) and come from the same publication with the same ancestry distribution, cohort list, and validation sample size, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is discounted). With endpoint and study context essentially tied, PGS005262 is better supported by stronger available PRS signal proxies: materially higher per-SD effect size (OR 1.41 vs 1.05; β 0.34 vs 0.05) and a slightly higher reported AUROC (0.593 vs 0.585). It also uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with far more variants (1,085,173 vs 110), which is a positive structural signal when PRS-only metrics are absent. Confidence is moderate because the key discrimination metric is full-model AUROC with unknown covariates for both.

Both candidates are from the same UKB portability paper, target the same endpoint mapping (trait_efo=nicotine dependence; trait_reported/phenotyping_reported=Tobacco use disorder), use similarly basic covariates, and have the same training (n=391,124 EUR) and validation size (n=19,400), so phenotype fidelity and study context are essentially tied. The differentiator is PRS signal strength and structural properties: PGS002037 shows higher PRS-comparable performance (partial-r 0.0741 vs 0.0557 for PGS001830) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with far more variants (847,691 vs 13,838), which is generally favorable for a polygenic trait when other fields are equal. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, partial-r plus the stronger genome-wide construction supports PGS002037.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo match; phenotyping_reported identical aside from a typo) and come from the same publication with the same evaluation ancestry mix and validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). With endpoint and validation context essentially tied, PGS005263 is better supported by stronger PRS signal proxies and structure: it has a much larger genome-wide score (1,085,170 variants) using PRSCS and shows a materially stronger per-SD effect size (OR≈1.36, β≈0.309) than PGS005261 (110 variants; OR≈1.05, β≈0.047). The tiny full-model AUROC difference (0.588 vs 0.585) is negligible, so the stronger effect size and genome-wide construction favor PGS005263.

Both candidates have good endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported are Osteoporosis), but PGS002768 is better-supported structurally and by study archetype: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants, whereas PGS001273 is a very sparse snpnet score (316 variants) from a pan-trait UK Biobank framework paper (“across 813 traits”), which domain guidance flags as typically less reliable for external generalization. Although PGS001273 reports explicit PRS-only AUROC/R² (0.5685; 0.00688), these are modest and its high full-model AUROC (0.7897) is largely covariate-driven (incremental AUROC only 0.00477). PGS002768 lacks PRS-only AUC/R² but provides a moderate per-SD effect size (OR 1.31, 1.25–1.38) in a cleaner, disease-focused comparative context and avoids the framework penalty, making it the stronger choice overall despite missing AUC/R².

PGS002768 is the better-supported choice for generic osteoporosis risk because its endpoint is a direct osteoporosis diagnosis (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Osteoporosis”) and it comes from a disease-focused cross-disease evaluation paper with clean basic covariates; it also reports a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.31, 95% CI 1.25–1.38) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with very large variant coverage (1,091,549). In contrast, PGS001274 is a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-framework score (“across 813 traits”) with a time-to-event, subtype-restricted endpoint (“osteoporosis without pathological fracture”), which is a fidelity mismatch for the broad target; while it reports PRS-only AUROC/R2 (0.576 / 0.00945), these are modest and the very high full-model AUROC is largely covariate-driven (small incremental AUROC 0.00777).

PGS005235 has tighter endpoint fidelity to the target obesity: despite a broader trait_reported label (“Adiposity”), its phenotyping_reported is explicitly “Obesity (phecode: 278.1)” with trait_efo=obesity, whereas PGS002033 uses a broader administrative bundle phenotype (“Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation”) and maps to multiple EFOs (obesity/overweight/overnutrition), which is less specific to obesity. On performance evidence, neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, but PGS005235 provides a strong PRS effect size (OR≈1.97), while PGS002033 only reports a modest partial correlation (partial-r≈0.079), which is weaker as discriminative evidence. Although PGS002033 has explicit training N and multi-ancestry evaluation, it comes from a UKB portability framework paper and its broader phenotype reduces confidence; overall the obesity-phecode anchoring plus stronger effect-size support makes PGS005235 better-supported here.

PGS001274 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance while remaining mapped to the same target EFO trait (osteoporosis). It reports higher PGS-only AUROC (0.57595 vs 0.5685) and higher PGS-only R² (0.00945 vs 0.00688) than PGS001273 under essentially identical covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), training sample (n=269,704), and evaluation setup/ancestry distribution. Although PGS001273 has a cleaner generic endpoint label (“Osteoporosis”) versus PGS001274’s time-to-event ‘osteoporosis without pathological fracture’, the endpoint mismatch is not large enough here to outweigh the consistently stronger PRS-only metrics and larger variant set in PGS001274 (1270 vs 316) within the same snpnet framework paper.

PGS005235 is better supported for the generic target trait obesity because its endpoint fidelity is strong despite the broader trait_reported label: phenotyping_reported is explicitly “Obesity (phecode: 278.1)” with trait_efo=obesity, and it comes from a disease/anthropometrics-focused multi-cohort context (EGG/GIANT/UKB) using a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto) with very large variant coverage (709,828) and a strong reported effect size (OR≈1.97 per SD). In contrast, PGS001298 is from a known pan-trait UKB sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”), uses a much sparser model (9,227 variants; snpnet), and its phenotype is time-to-event (“TTE obesity”), which is a less direct match for generic obesity status. Although PGS001298 reports PRS-only AUROC/R² (0.576/0.0115) that are heritability-plausible, these are modest and do not outweigh the framework + TTE endpoint penalties versus PGS005235’s stronger endpoint anchoring and effect-size evidence (despite missing AUC/R²).

PGS000549 is the better-supported choice for the target trait “ovarian neoplasm” because its concept alignment is exact (trait_efo = ovarian neoplasm; phenotyping_reported = malignant neoplasm of ovary), whereas PGS000082 maps to a narrower/different EFO concept (trait_efo = ovarian carcinoma) and uses an incident-only endpoint. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.567 in PGS000549 vs 0.656 in PGS000082) are not reliable for ranking—especially since PGS000082’s model is heavily covariate-augmented (includes family history and multiple reproductive/hormonal factors), making its discrimination less comparable to a standalone PRS. PGS000549 uses much cleaner/basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/batch), so its reported effects are less likely to be inflated by clinical packaging. PGS000082 has more variants (36 vs 16) and larger validation N, but those are secondary to endpoint fidelity and covariate comparability here.

PGS001255 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports PGS-only AUROC=0.6319 and PGS-only R2=0.01341 (both below the local h2_obs ceiling 0.0048 only in observed-scale nuance, but at least provides explicit PRS-only metrics), whereas PGS002046 provides no PGS-only AUC/R2 and only a small partial correlation (partial-r=0.0182), which is weaker and less directly interpretable for discrimination. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (otosclerosis), but PGS001255’s phenotyping is explicitly time-to-event (a mild mismatch penalty) while PGS002046 is generic diagnosis; however, the lack of comparable PRS-only metrics for PGS002046 outweighs that advantage. Both are UKB framework-style scores, but PGS002046’s genome-wide LDpred2 structure and larger variant count do not compensate for missing PRS-only metrics versus PGS001255’s explicit PRS-only AUROC/R2.

PGS000083 is the better-supported choice for the broad target trait “pancreatic carcinoma” because its endpoint is a general pancreatic cancer diagnosis (trait_efo: exocrine pancreatic carcinoma; phenotyping: incident pancreatic cancer) and it is evaluated cleanly in a clearly reported European validation (EVAL EUR 100%) with an explicit PRS-associated effect size (HR per SD 1.49). In contrast, PGS002264 is narrower (pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma only) and its reported AUROC=0.83 is a full-model metric paired with explicit clinical-risk packaging/mediator-like covariates (diabetes onset/age at DM diagnosis, waist circumference, family history, “clinical risk”), making the discrimination less attributable to the PRS and less comparable. Both lack PGS-only AUC/R2, so the covariate cleanliness and endpoint generality favor PGS000083 despite PGS002264’s higher full-model AUROC.

PGS000550 is the better-supported standalone PRS for the target ovarian neoplasm because its endpoint alignment is direct (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Malignant neoplasm of ovary” mapped to ovarian neoplasm) and its evaluation uses only basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs), making the reported effect size (OR 1.286 per SD) and AUROC less confounded by clinical risk-factor packaging. In contrast, PGS000082 has a close but not exact EFO mapping (“ovarian carcinoma”) and its reported discrimination comes from a much more covariate-heavy model including family history and multiple reproductive/hormonal factors, so its higher full-model AUROC (0.656 vs 0.568) is not comparable evidence of PRS quality. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the cleaner endpoint/covariate design of PGS000550 outweighs PGS000082’s larger validation sample.

PGS005217 is better supported for the target concept despite a slight label mismatch (peripheral artery disease vs peripheral vascular disease) because its phenotyping is a clear clinical endpoint (incident PAD) and it comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort study with broad multi-ancestry evaluation and a strong PRS-associated effect size (HR per SD 1.66). In contrast, PGS002055 is an exact-label match (peripheral vascular disease, unspecified) but is from a UKB portability framework paper and shows only a very weak PRS-comparable metric (partial-r 0.0175), with no AUC/R2/effect-size evidence of meaningful discrimination. Neither reports PGS-only AUC/R2, so the stronger endpoint-focused evidence package and effect-size signal favor PGS005217.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Parkinson’s disease) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROCs (0.651 for PGS000902 vs 0.80 for PGS001774) are not directly comparable as PRS metrics. PGS001774’s higher AUROC is further discounted because its model includes substantial non-genetic/clinical packaging covariates including family history, head injury, depression, smoking, and BMI, making the reported discrimination likely covariate-driven rather than PRS-driven. PGS000902 is supported by a large, disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis context with many contributing cohorts and uses only basic covariates (PCs, age, sex), and it has a much richer genetic component (90 variants vs 12), which is the more reliable structural signal given the lack of PRS-only metrics.

PGS003586 is the better-supported match to the target trait preeclampsia: its trait_reported is explicitly “Pre-eclampsia” with the same phenotyping_reported (“Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia”) as PGS003587, so endpoint fidelity favors A over B’s gestational-hypertension label (despite B mapping trait_efo to preeclampsia). Both candidates are near-clones in method (PRS-CS), training size (n=212,034), evaluation ancestry (EUR), covariates (maternal age, age^2, PCs), and validation N (25,582), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance differentiation relies on effect size: A shows a stronger OR per SD (1.31 vs 1.20 for B), indicating better PRS signal in the available comparable metric.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Malignant neoplasm of ovary”, trait_efo “ovarian neoplasm”), identical ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), same training cohort (UKB) and size (n=5,130), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation size (n=5,196). Given the near-clone setup, PGS000550 is better supported because it shows consistently slightly stronger PRS signal in the available evidence (higher Nagelkerke R² 0.0113 vs 0.00996 and higher per-SD OR 1.286 vs 1.263) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS with 1,115,189 variants) versus a sparse GWAS-hits score (16 variants) in PGS000549, which is generally less capable of capturing polygenic signal when all else is equal.

PGS005217 is better supported for the target peripheral vascular disease because it is a disease-focused PAD model with a clear diagnosis endpoint (“Incident peripheral artery disease”) and provides strong PRS signal evidence via an effect size (HR per SD 1.66, 95% CI 1.61–1.71) with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs). It is also developed/validated across many cohorts with broad multi-ancestry evaluation and a large validation sample (n=304,294), supporting transportability. In contrast, PGS001843 comes from a UKB portability framework paper, uses a very sparse 242-variant score, and its only PRS-comparable metric is a very small partial correlation (0.0151), with no AUC/R2/effect-size evidence; its phenotype is also vague (“Peripheral vascular disease, unspecified”), making it less clinically specific despite the exact trait_efo match.

PGS001298 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance and endpoint specificity for the target trait obesity. It reports explicit PGS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.57573; PGS R2 0.01146) with basic covariates and these are interpretable as PRS signal, whereas PGS002033 provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 (only partial correlation 0.0789) and has a broader, more composite phenotype label (“Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation”) that is less endpoint-faithful to obesity. Although PGS002033 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method with many more variants and slightly larger training N, the lack of directly comparable PRS-only metrics and the broader phenotype make it less well-supported than PGS001298 on the visible fields.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), identical covariates (basic demographics + PCs), identical training cohort and size (UKB, n=391,124), and identical ancestry distribution and validation sample size (n=19,668), so the decision rests on PRS-comparable performance and structural signals. PGS002055 shows a higher PRS-comparable metric (partial-r 0.0175 vs 0.0151 for PGS001843, with slightly higher CI bounds) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with far broader variant coverage (599,514 vs 242), which is generally favorable for polygenic disease architectures when other fields are matched. With no PGS-only AUC/R2 available for either, these modest but consistent advantages make PGS002055 better supported.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (Parkinson’s disease; same trait_efo and phenotyping_reported), come from the same publication, use the same basic covariates (PCs 1–5, age, sex), and have the same training sample size and validation N, so endpoint fidelity and study context do not differentiate them. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative; still, PGS000903 shows stronger supporting evidence than PGS000902: higher full-model AUROC (0.692 vs 0.651) plus additional effect-size evidence (β=0.709 and OR top vs bottom quartile=6.25 with CI), whereas PGS000902 provides only AUROC with no effect sizes. Overall, PGS000903 is better supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported pancreatic cancer; trait_efo exocrine pancreatic carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident pancreatic cancer), have identical ancestry evaluation (EUR 100%), identical variant count (22), and essentially identical reported discrimination/effect size (full-model AUROC 0.745; C-index ~0.742–0.743; HR 1.49) with the same covariate set including family history and smoking/BMI (so metrics are not clean PRS-only in either). PGS000794 is explicitly derived from PGS000083 but with inverse variant weights, which is a strong internal red flag for correctness/biological directionality rather than an evidence-backed improvement; its additional reported R²=0.439 is not labeled PRS-only and is implausibly high relative to the provided pancreatic cancer heritability ceiling (h2_obs ~0.057), suggesting non-comparable/full-model or mis-scaled reporting. Given near-tie otherwise, PGS000083 is better-supported as the original, coherent score without the inverse-weight anomaly.

PGS000794 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (pancreatic carcinoma) because it aligns well to the umbrella endpoint (trait_reported: pancreatic cancer; trait_efo: exocrine pancreatic carcinoma; phenotyping: incident pancreatic cancer) and provides PRS-relevant evidence via an effect size (HR per SD=1.49) with a largely standard epidemiologic covariate set (age/sex/PCs/array plus BMI and smoking), despite only reporting full-model discrimination. In contrast, PGS002264 targets the narrower subtype pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (a partial match to pancreatic carcinoma) and its reported AUROC=0.83 is from a clinically packaged model explicitly incorporating diabetes status/onset and family history (“clinical risk”), making the performance less comparable to standalone PRS quality; it also has evaluation ancestry not reported. Neither record reports PGS-only AUC/R2, so the decision rests on endpoint breadth and cleaner covariate context, favoring PGS000794.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Parkinson’s disease) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is not a reliable cross-model discriminator. PGS001774’s higher AUROC (0.80) is heavily discounted because its model includes substantial non-genetic/clinical packaging covariates including family history plus multiple risk factors (head injury, depression, smoking, BMI), making the reported AUROC likely covariate-driven and less comparable to a standalone PRS. PGS000903 is supported by a large disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis context with many variants (1805 vs 12) and cleaner/basic covariates (PCs, age, sex), and it provides additional PRS-relevant effect-size evidence (e.g., OR top vs bottom quartile 6.25; beta reported) without obvious clinical leakage. Overall, PGS000903 is the better-supported PRS candidate on the visible fields.

PGS003586 has clearly better endpoint fidelity to the target trait preeclampsia: its phenotyping_reported is "Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia" and trait_reported/efo both match preeclampsia, whereas PGS004593 is mapped to preeclampsia but its phenotyping_reported is "Gestational hypertension" (a related but non-identical hypertensive disorder of pregnancy). Both use PRS-CS with similar variant counts and basic covariates, so those do not differentiate; PGS004593’s larger validation N does not outweigh its phenotype mismatch and weaker effect size.

PGS003587 is better supported for the target trait preeclampsia because its endpoint fidelity is stronger: despite the broader trait_reported label (“Gestational hypertension”), its phenotyping_reported is explicitly “Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia,” aligning directly with preeclampsia, whereas PGS004593 has an exact trait_reported (“Preeclampsia”) but phenotyping_reported is “Gestational hypertension,” a clearer mismatch to the target. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so effect-size and study context matter more; PGS003587 shows a slightly stronger per-SD association (OR 1.20 vs HR 1.16 for PGS004593) and comes from a disease-focused Nat Med multi-cohort development with listed training cohorts and training N=212,034, while PGS004593 has N/A training details and appears more like an association/transport paper. PGS004593’s larger validation N does not outweigh its weaker phenotype alignment.

PGS001287 has cleaner, PRS-comparable performance evidence for psoriatic arthritis: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.67648 and PGS-only R2=0.0335 (and uses only basic covariates: age/sex/array/PCs), with endpoint mapping to psoriatic arthritis via phenotyping_reported “Psoriatic arthropathy.” Its PRS-only R2 is also below the provided liability h2 ceiling (0.0735), which is sanity-consistent. In contrast, PGS000342 is endpoint-faithful by label (“Psoriatic arthritis”) but provides only a full-model AUROC=0.562 with unknown covariates and no PGS-only AUC/R2, making its PRS contribution non-comparable and weakly supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all prostate cancer), study context (same publication), covariates (0), training cohort (UKB), training N (9,671), and evaluation ancestry mix (EUR/SAS) with the same validation N (171,474). Given otherwise identical design, these small but consistent advantages favor PGS004155, though the lack of PRS-only metrics keeps confidence below high.

PGS001313 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance and endpoint specificity: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.6729 with CI) and PGS-only R² (0.04966) for a psoriasis time-to-event phenotype with only basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs). Both are UKB-based framework/portability-style scores with multi-ancestry evaluation, so the decisive differentiator is the presence of explicit PRS-only metrics in PGS001313.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (prostate cancer), same publication/date, same training cohort (UKB) and training n=9,671, same ancestry distribution and validation sample size (n=171,474), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC/R² shown, which is not a clean PRS-comparable differentiator). Hence PGS004042 wins, but confidence is low due to the tiny differences and absence of PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to the target trait (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all psoriasis) and both are UKB-based framework-style scores, so phenotype fidelity does not differentiate. PGS001312 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.6916 with CI) and PGS-only R² (0.0523), whereas PGS002083 provides no AUROC/R² at all and only a partial correlation (0.0632), which is less directly comparable as a PRS discrimination metric. Although PGS002083 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method with many more variants (LDpred2; 71,744 vs 204) and larger training N, the lack of standard PRS-only AUC/R² evidence makes it harder to justify over PGS001312 given the selection policy that missing PGS-only AUC should not be substituted by other metrics.

PGS001030 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (pulmonary fibrosis) because it matches the umbrella endpoint directly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Pulmonary fibrosis”) and provides explicit PRS-only performance metrics (PGS AUROC 0.6252; PGS R2 0.0142). In contrast, PGS001791 targets the narrower subtype idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (endpoint mismatch vs the broader target) and, while it reports a covariates-regressed-out R2 (0.005929), it lacks a PRS-only AUROC and its PRS-only R2 is smaller. Although PGS001791 has a stronger structural setup (genome-wide PRS-CS-auto with many variants and multi-biobank development), the directly aligned phenotype plus clearer and stronger PRS-only metrics in PGS001030 outweigh that advantage here.

Both candidates are near-clone UKB snpnet sparse scores from the same pan-trait framework paper, with identical trait_efo (pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis), similar covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), and similar ancestry setup (DEV EUR; EVAL multi-ancestry with selected EUR performance). PGS001280 is the better-supported match to the target trait pulmonary embolism: its endpoint is explicitly PE with a time-to-event phenotyping (“TTE PE”) and trait_efo is pulmonary embolism only, whereas PGS001279 is a broader/mixed construct (trait_efo includes both pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis and is phrased as “previously: Blood clot in the lung,” which is closer to a history/self-report style label). On PRS-comparable metrics, PGS001280 has higher PGS-only AUROC (0.60765 vs 0.60034) and higher PGS-only R² (0.01403 vs 0.01146), with both well below the heritability ceiling, and covariates/ancestry context are essentially identical between the two. PGS001279’s larger validation N does not outweigh the weaker phenotype specificity and weaker PGS-only performance.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo both rheumatoid arthritis; phenotyping_reported both Seropositive RA), covariates (both 0), training cohort and size (UKB; n=820), ancestry distribution, and validation sample size (n=90,274). Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and context: same trait_reported/trait_efo (rheumatoid arthritis), same phenotyping_reported (Seropositive RA), same covariates (0), same training cohort (UKB) with the same small samples_training (n=820), identical ancestry_distribution, and identical validation_sample_size (n=90,274). PGS001312 is the better-supported choice for generic psoriasis risk because its endpoint is a direct psoriasis phenotype (phenotyping_reported: "Psoriasis") whereas PGS001313 is explicitly time-to-event ("TTE psoriasis" / "Psoriasis (time-to-event)"), which is a mild endpoint mismatch for a generic disease target. PGS001280 is the better match to the target trait pulmonary embolism because its endpoint is PE-only (trait_reported: "PE (time-to-event)"; phenotyping_reported: "TTE PE"; trait_efo: pulmonary embolism), whereas PGS001277 explicitly uses a composite phenotype ("PE +/- DVT") and maps to both pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis, reducing endpoint fidelity for PE specifically. Both candidates are otherwise near-clones (same snpnet framework paper, same training cohort/size, same covariates, same ancestry distribution and validation N), and both report clean PRS-only metrics; although PGS001277 has slightly higher PGS-only AUROC/R2 (0.611 vs 0.608; 0.0151 vs 0.0140), the difference is small and does not outweigh the clearer PE-specific phenotype alignment of PGS001280.

PGS000922 is the better-supported choice for generic sarcoidosis because it has clean, PRS-comparable performance reported (PGS-only AUROC=0.64282; PGS-only R2=0.01741) with only basic covariates, and its phenotype fields align directly to sarcoidosis (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Sarcoidosis”, trait_efo “sarcoidosis”). In contrast, PGS001872 has an endpoint mismatch signal (trait_efo “skin sarcoidosis” vs target sarcoidosis) and lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2 entirely (only partial correlation reported), making its predictive evidence less directly comparable despite more variants and larger training N.

PGS001137 is better-supported on PRS-comparable performance: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.573 and PGS-only R2=0.00663 (no covariates), which can be sanity-checked against the retinal detachment h2_obs ceiling (~0.0042) and interpreted directly as PRS signal. In contrast, PGS002040 provides no AUROC/R2 and only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0276), which is less directly comparable to standard PRS discrimination metrics. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (both map to EFO retinal detachment; PGS002040’s ‘detachments and defects’ is slightly broader), and both use only basic covariates, but PGS002040’s stronger structural features (LDpred2, genome-wide variants, larger training N) are not enough to outweigh the lack of PRS-only AUC/R2 evidence here.

Both candidates align to the target via the same mapped trait (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) and EUR evaluation ancestry, but PGS001791 has cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports a covariates-regressed-out/PGS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.005929 (below the pulmonary fibrosis h2_obs ceiling 0.0039–0.0164 range but at least interpretable as PRS signal), whereas PGS004695 provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 at all (only an HR high-vs-low quintile=3.78, which is less comparable across studies). Structurally, PGS001791 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS-auto) with ~910k variants and is developed across many biobanks, while PGS004695 is a 23-SNP genome-wide-significant score from an exposure-focused study context; with missing PRS-comparable metrics and a sparse construction, it is less well-supported as a standalone PRS for pulmonary fibrosis.

PGS000990 has cleaner, PRS-comparable performance evidence for the target trait: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.5415) and PGS-only R² (0.00213), which can be sanity-checked against the retinal detachment h2_obs ceiling (~0.0042) and are plausibly below it. It also provides incremental AUROC, helping interpret the full-model AUROC as largely covariate-driven. In contrast, PGS002040 lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R² entirely (only a partial correlation is given), making its predictive strength harder to judge on the catalog fields despite better endpoint wording and a genome-wide LDpred2 construction with many variants. Both are UKB-based framework/portability-style scores with broadly similar basic covariates and multi-ancestry evaluation, so the decisive advantage is PGS000990’s explicit PGS-only metrics versus PGS002040’s missing PRS-comparable discrimination metrics.

Both candidates are near-clones: same target trait/EFO, same phenotyping_reported (Seropositive RA), same covariates (0), same training cohort (UKB), same training n=820, same ancestry distribution and evaluation context, and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics shown, which are not ideal for PRS comparison). Given the small metric gaps and non-PRS-only nature of the AUC/R², confidence is moderate rather than high.

PGS000922 is the better match to the target trait sarcoidosis because its endpoint is the generic disease diagnosis (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: "Sarcoidosis"), whereas PGS000923 is explicitly a time-to-event formulation ("Sarcoidosis (time-to-event)", phenotyping_reported: "TTE sarcoidosis"), which is a noted endpoint-fidelity warning for a generic disease-risk target. Although PGS000923 has slightly higher PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.6456 vs 0.6428; PGS-only R2 0.018 vs 0.0174) and more variants (22 vs 12), both candidates share the same pan-trait UKB framework origin, identical training size, covariates, and ancestry distribution, making the small metric differences weak; thus phenotype alignment favors PGS000922.

PGS001030 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance and cleaner PRS evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.6252 and PGS-only R2=0.0142 (and incremental AUROC=0.01818), allowing direct PRS assessment and a heritability-ceiling sanity check, whereas PGS004695 provides no AUROC/R2 at all and only a quintile HR (3.78), which is less comparable across studies. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (pulmonary fibrosis vs idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; both map to pulmonary fibrosis spectrum), but PGS004695 is incident IPF and embedded in an exposure-focused study context, while PGS001030 is a direct pulmonary fibrosis PRS with standard genetic/demographic covariates and multi-ancestry evaluation metadata. Despite the known framework-paper penalty for the UKB ‘813 traits’ source of PGS001030, the absence of PRS-comparable metrics for PGS004695 makes it less well-supported overall.

PGS001137 is the better-supported choice for the target trait retinal detachment because it has cleaner endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to retinal detachment), whereas PGS000990 is explicitly a broader composite and time-to-event endpoint (“retinal detachments and breaks (time-to-event)”, phenotyping_reported “TTE retinal detachments and breaks”), which is a mild mismatch/packaging relative to the generic target. Both are otherwise near-clones (same pan-trait UKB framework paper, same training N, same covariates, same ancestry distribution and validation size), so the decision is driven by endpoint alignment plus the consistently better PGS-only performance for PGS001137. Both R2 values remain plausible relative to the local h2_obs ceiling (~0.0042), though PGS001137 is slightly above it, so confidence is not maximal.

PGS000923 is the better-supported choice for the target trait sarcoidosis because it has coherent endpoint mapping (trait_efo=sarcoidosis; phenotyping_reported=TTE sarcoidosis) and, critically, reports PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.64561 and PGS-only R²=0.018), allowing a clean PRS signal assessment and a heritability-ceiling sanity check. Both candidates are near-clones: same schizophrenia endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all schizophrenia), same publication, same method (PRS-CS), same evaluation ancestry (EUR 100%), and similarly basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, platform/batch), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match carcinoma in situ of skin), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), identical covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), same training cohort (MGI) and same training/validation sizes. Both candidates are near-clones: same schizophrenia endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), same method (PRS-CS), same ancestry distribution (GWAS mostly EUR with small EAS; EUR-only evaluation), and same basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/platform/batch) with no obvious leakage. Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match carcinoma in situ of skin), identical ancestry (EUR-only), same training cohort (MGI), same training N (6,005), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and same validation size (n=5,500). Both candidates are near-clones: same target endpoint (phenotyping_reported="Obstructive sleep apnea"; trait_efo="obstructive sleep apnea"), same publication/cohorts (FinnGen, MGBB, MVP), same covariates (including BMI), same evaluation ancestry mix and validation n=21,975, and both only report a full-model AUROC=0.79 (no PGS-only AUC/R2), so discrimination metrics are not cleanly comparable as PRS-only evidence. Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/efo/phenotyping all squamous cell carcinoma), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), same training cohort (MGI) and same validation N (8,473), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not clean PRS-comparable). Both candidates are near-clones for the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match thyroid cancer/carcinoma), same method (10 genome-wide significant variants) and same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry. Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match carcinoma in situ of skin), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sizes, and similarly basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either—so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative. With otherwise near-identical evidence and only a tiny AUROC difference (0.694 vs 0.692), the cleaner covariate set makes PGS000209 better-supported.

Both candidates align well to the target trait (sleep apnea) via obstructive sleep apnea and BMI-adjusted phenotyping, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so the full-model AUROC 0.79 in PGS005219 vs 0.77 in PGS003858 is not a reliable PRS-comparable differentiator). Given that, structural and effect-size evidence favors PGS005219: it is a genome-wide shrinkage/aggregation-style score with ~982,740 variants and reports a strong per-SD OR=1.98, whereas PGS003858 is a 6-SNP genome-wide-significant-hits score with only a small beta (0.066). Covariates are broadly similar (both include BMI, age, sex, PCs), and while PGS003858 has a larger validation n, validation size is a weak tie-break compared with the much stronger polygenic architecture capture and effect-size signal in PGS005219.

Both candidates align cleanly to the target (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are type 1 diabetes). PGS001297 has cleaner PRS-comparable metrics reported (PGS-only AUROC 0.771 and PGS-only R2 0.0912 with basic covariates), but it comes from a known pan-trait UK Biobank framework paper (“across 813 traits”), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external generalization. PGS000024 is disease-focused (T1DGC; newborn screening/incident diagnosis context) and shows broader multi-ancestry evaluation coverage in its ancestry_distribution, which is supportive for transportability, even though it only reports a full-model AUROC (0.921) and lacks PGS-only metrics (so that AUROC can’t be used as a PRS-only comparator). Given the strong penalty for framework-origin scores when a disease-focused alternative exists, PGS000024 is better-supported overall despite weaker metric cleanliness.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_efo is type 1 diabetes mellitus; phenotyping_reported is T1D/Type 1 diabetes). The key differentiator is PRS-comparable performance evidence: PGS001297 reports explicit PGS-only metrics (PGS AUROC(no covariates)=0.771 and PGS R2(no covariates)=0.0912), which are directly comparable and sit plausibly below the provided liability-scale heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.219). In contrast, PGS004162 provides only full-model AUROC/R² (and no PGS-only AUC/R²), so its discrimination cannot be attributed cleanly to the PRS per the policy guidance; despite having many more variants and strong OR per SD, the lack of PRS-only metrics makes it less well-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Squamous cell carcinoma”) and neither reports PRS-only AUROC/R2, so full-model AUROC (0.599 for PGS000461 vs 0.605 for PGS000731) is not a reliable differentiator—especially with different/unknown covariates. PGS000461 has cleaner, explicitly stated basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4) and provides richer validation reporting (AUROC with CI, pseudo-R², Brier, and top-1% OR), whereas PGS000731 has covariates listed as Unknown and provides only a point AUROC and per-SD OR. With comparable variant counts (13 vs 14) and both EUR-only evaluation, the better-supported and more transparent performance/covariate evidence favors PGS000461.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all schizophrenia), same method family (PRS-CS), same basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, platform/batch), and same ancestry context (GWAS mostly EUR with small EAS; EUR-only evaluation). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS-comparable metric; however, within this near-clone setting the higher reported AUROC favors PGS000135 (0.74, CI 0.67–0.81) over PGS000133 (0.60, CI 0.55–0.66). PGS000135 also has substantially more variants (972,439 vs 604,645), a positive structural signal within the same method. PGS000133’s OR=1.691 is supportive, but with no comparable PRS-only metrics and a lower AUROC, it does not outweigh the combined AUROC+variant-count advantage of PGS000135.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Squamous cell carcinoma”) and are EUR-only, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is not a clean differentiator). PGS000463 has more informative and better-specified evaluation metadata: explicit basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4) and additional performance evidence beyond AUROC, including Nagelkerke pseudo-R² (0.0268) and a strong tail-risk metric (OR top 1% vs rest = 3.74). In contrast, PGS000731 has unknown covariates and provides only a full-model AUROC plus a per-SD OR, making its reported discrimination harder to interpret as PRS-driven despite a larger validation sample and slightly higher AUROC. Therefore PGS000463 is better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo is type 1 diabetes mellitus; phenotyping_reported is T1D/Type 1 diabetes). However, PGS004162 provides cleaner PRS-relevant evidence: it explicitly uses no covariates (covariates=0) and reports effect sizes (OR per SD ~2.89 with CI) plus an R² estimate, whereas PGS000024 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.921) with covariates unknown and no PRS-only metrics/effect sizes, making its very high AUROC likely non-comparable and potentially covariate-driven. Although PGS000024 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation and a much larger stated validation sample size, the lack of PRS-isolated performance and unknown covariate package weakens support relative to PGS004162’s clearer standalone scoring context.

PGS000014 is the better-supported choice for generic type 2 diabetes mellitus risk because its endpoint is a direct T2D diagnosis (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Type 2 diabetes”), and it comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort development context (DIAGRAM/EPIC/GERA/UKB) with broad multi-ancestry evaluation listed. Although it lacks a PRS-only AUROC, it does report a PRS-comparable PGS-only R2=0.029 with only basic covariates. PGS001294 reports explicit PGS-only metrics (AUROC=0.6358, R2=0.0341) but is a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse framework score (“across 813 traits”, snpnet, 3,496 variants) and uses a time-to-event non-insulin-dependent diabetes phenotype, which is a weaker match to the generic T2D target and is a known generalization risk pattern versus disease-focused scores. The small R2 edge for PGS001294 does not outweigh the framework + TTE endpoint penalties.

PGS001306 is the better match to the target trait as a generic ulcerative colitis PRS: its trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are plain “Ulcerative colitis,” whereas PGS001307 is explicitly a time-to-event (TTE) endpoint (“Ulcerative colitis (time-to-event)”, “TTE ulcerative colitis”), which is a noted endpoint-fidelity penalty for a generic disease-risk target. On PRS-comparable metrics, PGS001307 is only marginally higher (PGS-only AUROC 0.638 vs 0.630; PGS-only R² 0.0238 vs 0.0204), a small gap that doesn’t outweigh the endpoint mismatch. Both are from the same pan-trait UKB framework paper, with identical training cohort/ancestry and similarly basic covariates, so those factors don’t differentiate them; validation size is larger for PGS001307 but is a weak tie-break compared with phenotype alignment.

Both candidates are near-clones for endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match thyroid cancer/carcinoma), method (GWAS-significant variants), variant count (10), and ancestry (EUR-only GWAS and evaluation) with the same covariates including family history (so neither has a covariate-clean PRS-only metric). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; only full-model AUROC is shown, which is discounted but can still separate siblings when everything else is effectively identical. On that limited comparable evidence, PGS000208 has higher reported AUROC (0.751 vs 0.692 for PGS000207) and also a much larger validation sample size (130,279 vs 3,137), while PGS000207’s extra development cohort (deCODE) is only a weak differentiator. Therefore PGS000208 is better-supported overall, though confidence is moderated because the key metric is full-model AUROC with family-history covariate inclusion.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and use only basic covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), so endpoint fidelity and leakage risk are similar. The key differentiator is that PGS001306 reports clean PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.63006 and PGS-only R²=0.02036, both interpretable and below the heritability ceiling), whereas PGS004253 provides no PGS-only AUC/R² and only a full-model AUROC=0.66 (not comparable as a standalone PRS metric). Although PGS004253 shows a strong per-SD OR (1.84) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with many variants, the lack of PRS-only performance reporting makes it less well-supported on the visible fields than PGS001306.

PGS002308 has higher endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both explicitly “Type 2 diabetes”), and comes from a disease-focused trans-ancestry T2D PRS development/validation study with broad multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/GME) and a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.96). In contrast, PGS001294 is from a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”) and uses a time-to-event non-insulin-dependent diabetes endpoint, which is a mild phenotype mismatch/packaging signal for generic T2D risk. Although PGS001294 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.636; R2=0.034) while PGS002308 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC/R2), the framework penalty and weaker endpoint fidelity make PGS002308 better-supported overall for type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported Bladder cancer; trait_efo urinary bladder carcinoma; phenotyping_reported Cancer of bladder), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), same training cohort/size (UKB; n=12,992), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation size (n=13,530). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only a weak within-family signal. Within this near-clone setting, PGS000613 shows consistently slightly stronger performance/effect evidence than PGS000611: higher AUROC (0.571 vs 0.567), higher pseudo-R² (0.0125 vs 0.0114), higher top-1% OR (2.91 vs 2.66), and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.301 vs 1.284), with similar CIs. With no other differentiators, these aligned improvements make PGS000613 better-supported.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate T2D) and neither shows obvious clinical-risk packaging beyond basic demographics/PCs. The key differentiator is PRS-comparable performance evidence: PGS000014 reports a PRS-only (covariate-adjusted) Nagelkerke R2=0.029, whereas PGS002308 provides only full-model metrics (AUROC=0.793, R2=0.092) without an explicit PGS-only AUC/R2, making its apparent advantage likely covariate-influenced and not directly comparable. PGS000014 also has clearly stated training cohorts and sample size (n=120,280; DIAGRAM/EPIC/GERA/UKB) and much broader evaluation ancestry coverage, while PGS002308 lists samples_training as N/A and fewer supporting records. Confidence is moderate because PGS002308 does report a strong OR per SD (1.96), but the lack of PRS-only metrics and missing training-scale detail weakens its support versus PGS000014.

PGS004253 is the better-supported ulcerative colitis PRS on endpoint fidelity and study archetype: it targets a direct UC diagnosis endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Ulcerative colitis”) and comes from a disease-focused UC paper, with a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto; 744,575 variants) and a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.84). In contrast, PGS001307 is a pan-trait UK Biobank framework score (“across 813 traits”) with a time-to-event phenotype (“TTE ulcerative colitis”), a very sparse model (809 variants; snpnet) and only modest PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC ~0.638; PGS R2 ~0.024). Although PGS001307 reports cleaner PRS-only AUC/R2 and broader evaluation ancestries, the framework+sparse+TTE endpoint combination is a consistent negative signal versus a disease-focused, direct-endpoint UC score with strong effect-size evidence; PGS004253’s missing PGS-only AUC/R2 keeps confidence from being high.

Both candidates match the target well (same trait_reported/trait_efo and identical phenotyping_reported and covariates; all EUR-only) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.571 vs 0.572) are essentially noise. PGS000613 is better supported by stronger PRS signal in the available effect-size evidence and tail discrimination: higher OR top 1% vs rest (2.91 vs 1.47) and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.301 vs 1.292), plus larger training (12,992 vs 7,469) and validation (13,530 vs 7,622). PGS000610’s only edge is a trivially higher full-model AUROC and pseudo-R², which are not PRS-comparable here.

PGS001536 is better supported for vitiligo because it has clear endpoint alignment (trait_efo=Vitiligo; phenotyping_reported explicitly “TTE vitiligo”) and, crucially, reports PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193 and PGS-only R2=0.01621) with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, array), staying well below the vitiligo heritability ceiling. It also has explicit training context (UKB; n=269,704) and broader evaluation ancestries listed. In contrast, PGS000738 has a major endpoint/phenotype incoherence: phenotyping_reported is “Red hair,” which does not match vitiligo, and it lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only a pseudo R²/full-model-style metric is shown), making its predictive evidence much less comparable despite the disease-focused publication title.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target trait (same trait_reported/trait_efo, same phenotyping_reported, same method_name and variants_number=13, and EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL with the same basic covariates), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC/Nagelkerke R²), so performance comparability is limited. PGS000610 has a trivially higher full-model AUROC (0.572 vs 0.567) and pseudo-R² (0.013 vs 0.0114), but these small differences are essentially noise given identical covariate structure and lack of PRS-only metrics; its top-1% OR is also weaker and imprecise (1.47, CI crosses 1) versus PGS000611 (2.66, tighter CI). With endpoint fidelity tied, I favor PGS000611 for stronger risk stratification evidence (top 1% vs rest OR) and slightly larger training/validation sample sizes, though the overall separation is small hence low confidence.

Both candidates align well to the target uterine cancer via endometrial carcinoma endpoints (PGS003381: uterine endometrial carcinoma; PGS000075: incident endometrial cancer; both map to EFO endometrial carcinoma). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the similar full-model AUROCs (0.761 vs 0.755) are not decisive and are not directly comparable as PRS metrics. PGS003381 is better-supported structurally and for comparability: it is a genome-wide lassosum score with very large variant count (529,365) and only basic covariates (age, PCs), whereas PGS000075 is a 9-variant GWAS-hits score and its reported performance is bundled with many clinical/epidemiologic covariates including family history and reproductive/hormonal factors, making the full-model AUROC less informative about PRS contribution. Despite PGS000075 having a larger validation N and an HR=1.19, the heavy covariate packaging and extreme sparsity make it less convincing as a standalone PRS for uterine cancer than PGS003381.

Both candidates are essentially matched on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Urinary calculus”, trait_efo urolithiasis), study context (same UKB portability paper), training sample size (n=391,124), covariates (sex, age, birth date, deprivation index, 16 PCs), and validation setup (same multi-ancestry distribution; selected European validation; n=19,913). With PRS-only AUC/R2 absent for both, the main differentiators are the PRS-comparable metric available and structural properties: PGS002075 shows a higher partial correlation (0.0385 vs 0.0323 for PGS001864) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with far more variants (731,196 vs 5,599), which is generally favorable for capturing polygenic signal when other fields are tied. Therefore PGS002075 is better supported on the visible evidence.

PGS004563 is better supported for the target urolithiasis because its endpoint is a specific ICD-style diagnosis code for kidney/ureter stones (phenotyping_reported: N20), which is a direct clinical instantiation of urolithiasis/nephrolithiasis, and it provides a PRS effect size (OR=1.283) giving at least some discriminative evidence. In contrast, PGS001864 comes from a UKB portability/framework-style paper (“Portability of 245 polygenic scores…”) and only reports a weak partial correlation (partial-r=0.0323) with no PRS-only AUC/R2 or effect size, making its performance evidence thinner despite broader multi-ancestry evaluation. Both are UKB-derived and EUR-trained, but the combination of more disease-specific endpoint coding plus an interpretable OR favors PGS004563.

PGS001536 is the better-supported vitiligo PRS because its endpoint is directly vitiligo (phenotyping_reported: "TTE vitiligo") and it reports PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.64193; PGS-only R2 0.01621), which are interpretable and below the vitiligo heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.174). It also has broader evaluation ancestry coverage (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS) with a large validation sample (n=67,425) and only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array). In contrast, PGS000760 has a major phenotype mismatch despite the vitiligo label: phenotyping_reported is "anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients" (treatment-induced, different endpoint), provides no PRS AUC/R2 (only an HR 1.41), and is validated on a much smaller sample (n=1,584), making it far less reliable for generic vitiligo risk prediction.

Both candidates align well to the target uterine cancer via endometrial carcinoma/cancer (dominant uterine subtype) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC (0.761 vs 0.754) is not a reliable differentiator—especially because PGS000786’s model is heavily covariate-packaged (family history plus multiple reproductive/hormonal/BMI factors), making its reported discrimination less comparable to standalone PRS performance. PGS003381 uses only basic covariates (age, PCs), avoiding that leakage/packaging concern, and is a genome-wide lassosum score with very large variant count (529,365) versus PGS000786’s 9-variant construction, which is structurally less likely to capture polygenic signal. Given cleaner covariates and stronger PRS structure, PGS003381 is better supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates align well to the target (uterine cancer) via the dominant subtype endpoint: trait_reported/trait_efo are identical (endometrial cancer / endometrial carcinoma) and phenotyping_reported is the same (incident endometrial cancer), with identical evaluation ancestry (EUR) and validation size (n=212,156) and essentially identical full-model AUROC/C-index and HR (PGS000075 AUROC 0.755, HR 1.19; PGS000786 AUROC 0.754, HR 1.18). However, PGS000786 is explicitly a derivative of PGS000075 (“9 variants from Graff et al (PGS000075) with inverse variant weights”), i.e., not an independently developed score and even suggests a potentially incorrect sign convention. It also reports an R²=0.486 that is not labeled PRS-only and is implausibly high relative to the provided uterine-cancer heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0116), making that metric non-comparable/suspect. With no PRS-only AUC/R² available for either, the cleaner, original source score (PGS000075) is better-supported than a sign-inverted repackage (PGS000786).

PGS000760 is better supported on PRS-relevant evidence despite both having the same trait_reported/trait_efo (vitiligo). Endpoint fidelity is weak for both, but PGS000760’s phenotyping_reported (anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients) is at least a clinically defined immune-related adverse event context, whereas PGS000738’s phenotyping_reported is clearly incoherent for vitiligo (“Red hair”), suggesting metadata contamination or proxy phenotype. On performance evidence, neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; however PGS000760 provides an interpretable PRS effect size (HR=1.41 per SD, moderate signal) with basic covariates (5 genotype PCs), while PGS000738 only shows a beta and a pseudo R² (0.0386) that appears to be a full-model/unclear metric and offers no clean PRS-only discrimination. Training/development support is also clearer for PGS000760 (UKB; samples_training n=408,959) versus PGS000738 (samples_training N/A). Overall, PGS000760 has more coherent supporting fields and less obviously mismatched phenotyping than PGS000738.

PGS004563 is better supported for urolithiasis because its endpoint is a specific ICD-coded kidney/ureter stone phenotype (phenotyping_reported: N20 calculus of kidney and ureter; trait_efo: nephrolithiasis), which is a close clinical match to the target and more specific than PGS002075’s broader “Urinary calculus” portability-framework phenotype. While neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, PGS004563 at least provides an effect size (OR=1.283 per SD), whereas PGS002075 only reports a small partial correlation (partial-r=0.0385), offering weaker evidence of discriminative signal. PGS002075 does have broader multi-ancestry evaluation, but given the stronger endpoint specificity and more interpretable PRS effect-size evidence, PGS004563 is the stronger choice overall.
